nuance.biblical_note: Jazer is a town east of the Jordan in the region of Gilead. Numbers 21:32 (RSV) records Israel capturing Jazer during the journey toward the land. Numbers 32:35 (RSV) names it among towns rebuilt by the Gadites, and Joshua 21:39 (RSV) assigns it to the Levites.

core.definition: A king of Judah who reigned briefly in 597 BC before being taken into exile in Babylon; also called Jehoiachin.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, 'NYE'. The last syllable is a weak 'uh' sound, not a full 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans encounter this name in Bible reading, church history and genealogy. The Revised Standard Version uses Jechoniah in Matthew 1 and Jeconiah or Jehoiachin elsewhere, so check which spelling your Bible uses.

distinctions.note: Both names refer to the same king; Jehoiachin appears in Kings, while Jeconiah appears in Chronicles and Jeremiah's variants.

examples.everyday: Someone in my study group asked who Jeconiah was, and I explained he is the same king as Jehoiachin.
examples.professional: In my lesson on the exile, I cover Jeconiah's three-month reign and his deportation to Babylon.
examples.analytical: Jeremiah 22:24-30 pronounces judgment on Jeconiah, which raises questions about how the royal line and the promise to David were understood after 597 BC.

nuance.analogy: Think of him as a leader whose name changes in different records, like a person who goes by two titles in two different documents.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yekonyah, meaning Yahweh establishes, a form related to Jehoiachin.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in JEK-uh-nye-uh.
Thinking Jeconiah and Jehoiachin are two different kings.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Yekonyah means Yahweh establishes. He is also called Jehoiachin (Yehoyakin). 2 Kings 24:8-15 records his brief reign and his surrender to Nebuchadnezzar in 597 BC, followed by deportation to Babylon. 2 Kings 25:27-30 reports that Evil-merodach released him from prison and gave him a regular allowance. Jeremiah 22:24 calls him Coniah and foretells that he will not have a son who sits on David's throne. Matthew 1:11-12 includes him in Jesus' genealogy, where the RSV spells the name Jechoniah.

senses.definition: A collimated stream, spurt or flow of liquid or gas from a pressurized container, an engine, etc.
senses.example: The fire extinguisher released a powerful jet of foam across the kitchen floor.

senses.definition: A spout or nozzle for creating a jet of fluid.
senses.example: The garden hose has a brass jet that lets me adjust the water pressure.

senses.definition: A type of airplane using jet engines rather than propellers.
senses.example: We flew to Denver on a jet that left Boston just after noon.

senses.definition: An engine that propels a vehicle using a stream of fluid as propulsion. A turbine.
senses.example: The engineers replaced the jet on the test aircraft after it overheated during the flight.

senses.definition: A turbine.
senses.example: The microturbine jet in our lab generates electricity from the exhaust gases.

senses.definition: A rocket engine.
A part of a carburetor that controls the amount of fuel mixed with the air.
senses.example: When the carburetor jet clogs, the engine idles roughly and stalls at stoplights.

senses.definition: A hard, black form of coal, sometimes used in jewelry.
senses.example: She wore a black jet bracelet that her grandmother had owned since the 1920s.

senses.definition: The color of jet coal, deep gray.
senses.example: jet:

senses.definition: An operation that takes a differentiable function f and produces a polynomial, the Taylor polynomial (truncated Taylor series) of f, at each point of its domain.
senses.example: The n-th jet of a smooth function f is its Taylor polynomial at each point.

senses.definition: A narrow cone of hadrons and other particles produced by the hadronization of a quark or gluon.
senses.example: In the collider data, each quark produced a narrow jet of hadrons traveling in one direction.

senses.definition: (dated) Drift; scope; range, as of an argument.
senses.example: The jet of his argument was far broader than the committee had expected.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) The sprue of a type, which is broken from it when the type is cold.
senses.example: The printer snapped the jet off each cold piece of type before inking.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To spray out of a container.
senses.example: The cleaner jets a fine mist of solution onto the window glass.

senses.definition: To spray with liquid from a container.
senses.example: Farmers may either dip or jet sheep with chemicals.

senses.definition: To travel on a jet aircraft or otherwise by jet propulsion.
senses.example: We jetted to Chicago on Thursday and were home before midnight.

senses.definition: To move (running, walking etc.) rapidly around.
senses.example: Kids jetted around the playground, shrieking and chasing each other.

senses.definition: To shoot forward or out; to project; to jut out.
senses.example: A rocky ledge jetted out over the river, shading the path below.

senses.definition: To strut; to walk with a lofty or haughty gait; to be insolent; to obtrude.
senses.example: The arrogant sales manager jetted down the hallway as if he owned the building.

senses.definition: To jerk; to jolt; to be shaken.
To adjust the fuel to air ratio of a carburetor; to install or adjust a carburetor jet.
To leave; depart.
senses.example: Gotta jet. See you tomorrow.

senses.definition: Propelled by turbine engines.
senses.example: jet airplane

senses.definition: Very dark black in color.

core.definition: A forceful, narrow stream of liquid or gas pushed out through a small opening, such as from a hose, nozzle or engine.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short e, as in 'bet', not a long 'jeet'. The final t is a crisp stop, not a flap, when it ends a word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It suggests force and speed, which can be positive in engineering and cleaning contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'jet' for a forceful stream from a sprayer, faucet, nozzle or engine, often in technical or cleaning talk. In everyday conversation, 'jet' for an airplane is very common, as in 'jet to Denver', but the sense of a stream is more specialized. For a gentle stream, Americans usually say 'stream' or 'spray' instead.

distinctions.note: A spray is a fine mist of many droplets, while a jet is a narrow, forceful stream.
A stream is a continuous flow of any strength; a jet is narrow and driven hard by pressure.

examples.everyday: Hold the hose close to the window, because the water jet is strong enough to crack the old paint.
examples.professional: The new injector nozzle sends a fine fuel jet directly into the combustion chamber, which improves efficiency.
examples.analytical: Newton's third law explains rocket propulsion: the jet of exhaust pushed backward generates a reaction force that moves the vehicle forward.

nuance.analogy: Like water shooting out of a garden hose when you put your thumb over the end.
nuance.etymology: From Old French jeter, meaning 'to throw'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long vowel, 'jeet', which sounds like a different word.
Confusing 'jet' with 'spray' when the stream is gentle or wide.

jet.etymology: French *jet* (“spurt”), from Old French *get*, *giet*, from Vulgar Latin **iectus, *jectus*, from Latin *iactus* (“a throwing, a throw”), from *iacere* (“to throw”).

senses.definition: Items thrown overboard from a ship or boat in distress in order to lighten its load.
senses.example: There she was, floating amongst the jetsam, like so much debris.

senses.definition: Discarded or leftover odds and ends.
senses.example: They were the jetsam of the dot-com bust.

core.definition: Cargo or equipment thrown overboard from a ship in danger to make it lighter, or things that have been discarded and left behind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second syllable a reduced schwa, like 'sum'. Do not confuse it with 'flotsam', which is the sound-alike partner word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, suggesting waste, loss or castoffs.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use jetsam mostly in nautical writing or in literary and figurative speech. It almost always appears in the fixed pair 'flotsam and jetsam', meaning scattered odds and ends or debris. In everyday conversation people usually say 'junk', 'leftovers' or 'stuff'.

distinctions.note: Jetsam is thrown overboard deliberately; flotsam floats on the water after a ship has sunk or broken apart.
Debris is a general word for scattered broken remains, while jetsam suggests objects deliberately discarded.

examples.everyday: After the move, the garage was full of the flotsam and jetsam of twenty years of family life.
examples.professional: The migration left behind jetsam: outdated tables, orphaned scripts and configuration files nobody had documented.
examples.analytical: Historians often study the cultural jetsam of an era, such as forgotten pamphlets and failed policies, to see what a society chose to discard.

nuance.analogy: Like the things a ship throws over the side in a storm to stay afloat: heavy, unwanted, and left behind for the sea.
nuance.etymology: Short for jettison, from Anglo-French getteson, from Old French jeter, meaning 'to throw'.
common_mistakes: Using jetsam alone in everyday speech, where it sounds bookish; 'flotsam and jetsam' is the natural phrase.
Confusing jetsam with flotsam, which means floating wreckage rather than discarded cargo.

core.definition: A Hebrew personal name meaning Yahweh has been gracious; in the Bible, a Judean military leader who opposed Gedaliah's rule after the fall of Jerusalem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, HAH. The initial sound is a j as in 'joy', and the final syllable is a weak 'nuhn'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a personal name and a biblical name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet Johanan in Bible study or church settings. In English it is often spelled John or Jonathan, and in daily life people rarely use this form.

distinctions.note: John is the common English form of the same Hebrew name; Johanan is a more literal transliteration used in certain biblical contexts.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study, someone asked who Johanan was, and the leader explained he was a military leader after Jerusalem fell.
examples.professional: The commentary on Jeremiah 40 identifies Johanan as the man who warned Gedaliah of a plot.
examples.analytical: The narrative presents Johanan as a figure of loyalty and suspicion, and his counsel is rejected with disastrous results.

nuance.analogy: Johanan is like an old family name that appears in many branches of the family tree, each with its own story.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Yohanan, meaning Yahweh has been gracious.
common_mistakes: Confusing Johanan with John the Baptist or John the Apostle, who are different people.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew yohanan, meaning Yahweh has been gracious. Johanan son of Kareah appears in the book of Jeremiah as a Judean officer after the fall of Jerusalem. Key passages: Jeremiah 40:13-16 describes him warning Gedaliah about a plot against him; Jeremiah 41:11-16 tells how he rescues the captives from Ishmael; Jeremiah 43:2-5 shows him leading the people to Egypt against the prophet's counsel.

senses.definition: To profit from a craze; to join a trend.
senses.example: After the incredible success of Wonka's latest low-fat chocolate bar, Fickelgruber has jumped on the bandwagon, and released a low-fat version.

core.definition: To join a popular trend, movement, or craze after it is already successful, often for personal gain.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BAND in the compound 'bandwagon', and 'the' is reduced to 'thuh' before a consonant. The final syllable of 'wagon' is a weak 'uhn'.

nuance.connotation: Negative to neutral. It usually suggests opportunism or late, self-interested participation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom about companies, politicians, or people who join a trend only once it is popular. It is often mildly critical, as in 'Every brand jumped on the bandwagon with AI slogans.' A natural reply is 'Yeah, everyone's doing it now.'

distinctions.note: Follow the crowd describes general conformity, while jump on the bandwagon implies joining a trend for personal gain or popularity.
An early adopter starts using something first, while someone who jumps on the bandwagon joins late, after it is popular.

examples.everyday: My brother bought a smart watch just because everyone else jumped on the bandwagon.
examples.professional: Several vendors jumped on the bandwagon with generative AI features, but few have solved the underlying data quality problems.
examples.analytical: The essay shows how public opinion can jump on the bandwagon of a popular idea without testing its evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like arriving at a parade after the band has started and climbing up onto the wagon to ride along.
nuance.etymology: From a wagon carrying a band in parades and circuses, later applied in American politics to joining the apparent winner.
common_mistakes: Using 'in the bandwagon' instead of 'on the bandwagon'.
Using the idiom as a neutral compliment; it usually implies opportunism.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to jurisprudence.
senses.example: Her jurisprudential argument rested on the original meaning of the due process clause.

core.definition: Relating to the philosophy or theory of law, including how laws should be understood and applied.

pronunciation.tip: The stress shifts from PROO in jurisprudence to DEN in the -ial form. Keep the vowels in the first syllables light and reduced, and say the -tial as 'shul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise academic term and sounds scholarly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use jurisprudential mainly in law schools, legal philosophy and academic writing. You would hear it in a seminar or read it in a law review article. In casual talk, people would say 'the philosophy of law' instead.

distinctions.note: Judicial concerns the work of judges and courts, while jurisprudential concerns the theory and philosophy behind the law.
Case law is the body of past court decisions, while jurisprudence is the study or theory of what law is and how it should be interpreted.

examples.everyday: My roommate in law school keeps talking about jurisprudential debates, and I just nod along.
examples.professional: The memo summarizes the jurisprudential basis for our data-retention policy.
examples.analytical: Hart's critique of Austin raises jurisprudential questions about whether legal validity depends on moral content.

nuance.analogy: Like a coach studying why the rulebook exists, not just what the rules say.
nuance.etymology: From Latin iurisprudentia, from ius (law) and prudentia (knowledge, skill).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable of jurisprudential, when the main stress falls on DEN.
Confusing jurisprudence, the theory of law, with judiciary, the system of courts and judges.

senses.definition: An instrument consisting of a tube containing mirrors and loose, colorful beads or other objects; when the tube is looked into and rotated, a succession of symmetrical designs can be seen.
senses.example: As a child, I spent hours turning the kaleidoscope and watching colored glass shift.

senses.definition: A constantly changing series of colors or other things.
A swarm of butterflies.
senses.example: Walking through the meadow, we saw a kaleidoscope of butterflies rising from the milkweed.

senses.definition: To move in shifting (and often attractive or colorful) patterns.
senses.example: Sunlight through the stained glass kaleidoscopes across the pews every morning.

core.definition: A tube with mirrors and loose colored pieces that forms changing symmetrical patterns; also, any constantly changing mix of colors or things.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, LY, and the first and third syllables are weak. Learners often give the first syllable too much force or stress the final syllable; the last syllable is 'skohp,' not 'skope.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests bright, shifting beauty and variety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use kaleidoscope both for the toy and, more often, as a metaphor for a rapidly changing mix of colors, people, or events. It is common in descriptions of scenery, crowds, cities, and art. It is slightly poetic, so in technical or business talk, say 'mix' or 'range' instead.

distinctions.note: A prism splits light into a fixed spectrum, while a kaleidoscope creates changing, symmetrical patterns from reflections and moving objects.
A mosaic is a fixed picture made of small pieces, while a kaleidoscope emphasizes constant change and movement.

collocations: the market is a kaleidoscope of options

examples.everyday: The farmers market was a kaleidoscope of colors this morning, with peppers, flowers, and bright scarves everywhere.
examples.professional: Our customer data is a kaleidoscope of formats, so the first step is standardizing the fields before we build the dashboard.
examples.analytical: Wallace Stevens presents a kaleidoscope of perception in which the self constantly reassembles the world into new patterns.

nuance.analogy: A kaleidoscope is like a snow globe that you keep turning, where every twist gives you a new arrangement of the same bright pieces.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kalos, 'beautiful,' eidos, 'form,' and skopein, 'to look at,' coined in English in the 1810s.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying KAL-uh-scope instead of kuh-LY-duh-skohp.
Using 'kaleidoscope' for a single fixed image instead of something that keeps changing.

core.definition: A patriarch in the early genealogy of Genesis, son of Enosh and father of Mahalalel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KEE. The second syllable is a reduced "uhn," like the end of "button."

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Kenan is used in Bible study, genealogies, and church teaching. Americans would say it mainly when reading Genesis or discussing names in the Bible. It is also a personal name in some American families.

distinctions.note: Cainan is the Greek spelling used in Luke 3:37 in the Revised Standard Version, while Kenan is the Hebrew form in Genesis.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's Bible has a family tree, and Kenan is one of the early names on it.
examples.professional: In the church education course, we listed the patriarchs, starting with Adam, Seth, Enosh, and Kenan.
examples.analytical: The genealogy of Kenan in Genesis 5 links the descendants of Seth to Noah, creating a chronological structure within the primeval history.

nuance.analogy: Like a link in a long chain of family names, passed from one generation to the next.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the name as "KEN-an," with a short vowel, instead of "KEE-nun."
Confusing Kenan with Cain or with Canaan, which are different names.
nuance.biblical_note: Kenan appears in the genealogy of Seth in Genesis 5:9-14, where he is the son of Enosh and father of Mahalalel. He is also listed in 1 Chronicles 1:2 in the RSV. In Luke 3:37, the RSV uses the Greek form Cainan in the genealogy of Jesus, which is a different link in the chain of descent.

senses.definition: The branch of mechanics concerned with motion of objects, as well as the reason i.e. the forces acting on such bodies. This, along with kinematics constitute dynamics, which is concerned purely with the effects of forces on moving bodies.
senses.example: In physics class we studied kinetics to predict how the cart would accelerate down the ramp.

senses.definition: The branch of chemistry that is concerned with the rates of chemical reactions.

core.definition: The branch of mechanics that studies the forces that produce or change motion. In chemistry, it means the study of reaction rates.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, NET, and the first and last syllables are reduced. The final -ics is pronounced /ɪks/ with a short i, not /aɪks/.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Physicists, engineers and chemists use kinetics when they need the causes of motion, not just its description. In chemistry, reaction kinetics is standard vocabulary in labs and papers. In everyday talk, Americans would say physics or how things move instead.

distinctions.note: Kinematics describes motion through position, velocity and acceleration without asking what causes it. Kinetics adds the forces that produce or change the motion.
Dynamics is the broader field that includes both kinematics and kinetics, so kinetics is one part of dynamics.
Kinetic energy is a quantity, the energy an object has because it is moving. Kinetics is the field of study.

examples.everyday: My son asked why the ball keeps rolling, so I tried to explain kinetics and lost him in about ten seconds.
examples.professional: Our reaction kinetics model did not match the lab data, so we refit the rate constants before the review.
examples.analytical: Kinetics asks not merely how a body moves but which forces bring that motion about and how they change it.

nuance.analogy: Kinematics is the choreography of a dance; kinetics is the push and pull of the dancers' muscles that make each step happen.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kinētikos, 'moving', from kinein, 'to move'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ics as /aɪks/ instead of /ɪks/.
Using kinetics to mean kinetic energy, the energy of motion itself.
Confusing kinetics with kinematics, which leaves out forces.

senses.definition: A male monarch; a man who heads a monarchy; in an absolute monarchy, the supreme ruler of his nation.
senses.example: Henry VIII was the king of England from 1509 to 1547.

senses.definition: The monarch with the most power and authority in a monarchy, regardless of sex.
senses.example: The king addressed his people from the balcony of the palace on the morning of his coronation.

senses.definition: A powerful or majorly influential person; someone who holds the preeminent position.
senses.example: Howard Stern styled himself as the "king of all media".

senses.definition: Something that has a preeminent position.
senses.example: In times of financial panic, cash is king.

senses.definition: A man worthy of respect.
senses.example: I'm sure you got the job, king.

senses.definition: A component of certain games.
senses.example: Before the game starts, each player places their king token on the starting square of the board.

senses.definition: A playing card with the letter "K" and the image of a king on it, the thirteenth card in a given suit.
senses.example: She laid down the king of hearts and won the trick with it.

senses.definition: A checker (a piece of checkers/draughts) that reached the farthest row forward, thus becoming crowned (either by turning it upside-down, or by stacking another checker on it) and gaining more freedom of movement.
senses.example: My opponent sacrificed a piece so that he could get a king on the back row.

senses.definition: The central pin or skittle in bowling games.
senses.example: Her ball hit the king pin dead center, knocking down nearly all the pins.

senses.definition: Senses related to animals.
A male dragonfly; a drake.
senses.example: The biologist said the largest dragonfly on the pond was a king guarding his territory.

senses.definition: A chinook salmon (king salmon).
senses.example: Anglers on the Kenai River hooked a king that weighed nearly forty pounds.

senses.definition: A group of animals whose tails have become entangled.
senses.example: A king of rats was discovered in the attic, their tails knotted together.

senses.definition: Senses related to large sizes of certain items A king skin.
senses.example: Oi mate, have you got kings?

senses.definition: A king-sized bed.
senses.example: We bought a king for the master bedroom so we could finally stretch out.

senses.definition: A vertex in a directed graph which can reach every other vertex via a path with a length of at most 2.
senses.example: In the directed graph, node A is a king because it reaches every other vertex within two steps.

senses.definition: The principal chess piece, that players seek to threaten with unavoidable capture to result in a victory by checkmate. It is often the tallest piece, with a symbolic crown with a cross at the top.
senses.example: He sacrificed his queen to expose the king and force checkmate in three moves.

senses.definition: A reproductive caste of termites comprising males who remain in the colony mating with the queen and releasing pheromones that manage the other castes in the colony.
senses.example: The colony's king stays beside the queen for life, helping her lay eggs.

senses.definition: (historical) A male leader of a traditional Aboriginal group, often used as a title by colonists.
senses.example: In colonial records, the local king was often a man chosen to deal with settlers.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To crown king, to make (a person) king.
senses.example: The bishops gathered in the cathedral to king the young prince before the crowd.

senses.definition: To rule over as king.
senses.example: For thirty years, he kinged the northern valley before the rebellion finally toppled him.

senses.definition: To perform the duties of a king.
To assume or pretend preeminence (over); to lord it over.
To promote a piece of draughts/checkers that has traversed the board to the opposite side, that piece subsequently being permitted to move backwards as well as forwards.
To dress and perform as a drag king.

core.definition: A man who rules a country as its monarch, holding the highest position of authority in a kingdom.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable, with a short 'i' like in 'sit'. Make sure the final 'ng' is a single nasal sound, not 'ng' plus a 'g' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, with a strong sense of power and authority. Figurative uses can be positive or negative, depending on whether the person is admired or resented.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use king in everyday talk for literal monarchs, in fairy tales, history and sports or pop culture phrases like 'king of the hill' or 'king of rock.' The United States has no king, so Americans often refer to real kings with an explanation, such as 'the king of Spain.' For a powerful person, 'the boss' or 'the top dog' is more casual.

distinctions.note: Monarch is the general term for any sovereign ruler, including queens and emperors, while king specifically refers to a male ruler.
An emperor rules an empire, often over several kingdoms or peoples, while a king usually rules a single kingdom.
Ruler is a broad term for anyone who governs, including presidents, while king refers only to a hereditary monarch.

examples.everyday: My little brother walks around the yard acting like he's the king of the hill.
examples.professional: The team lead joked that the senior engineer was the king of the release pipeline.
examples.analytical: Medieval political theory often presented the king as the living embodiment of the realm's justice and order.

nuance.analogy: A king is like the captain of a ship: he has the final say, but he works within a larger crew and a set of traditions.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cyning, from Proto-Germanic kuningaz, meaning 'man of the people' or 'descendant of the nobility'.
common_mistakes: Using king for a female ruler; use queen instead.
Pronouncing the 'g' at the end of 'king', which is silent in standard American speech.

king.etymology: From Middle English *king*, *kyng*, *kynge*, from Old English *cening*, *cing*, *cining*, *cuning*, *cyncg*, *cyneg*, *cyng*, *cyngc*, *cynig*, *cyning*, *king*, *kining*, *kuning*, *kyning*, *kyningc* (“king”), from **kuning*, from Proto-Germanic…

senses.definition: To hit or collide with.
senses.example: As I took the can off the shelf, I knocked down the one beside it.

senses.definition: To hit or knock (something or someone), intentionally or accidentally, so that it falls.
senses.example: As I took the can off the shelf, I knocked down the one beside it.

senses.definition: To demolish.
senses.example: We knocked down the garden shed when we moved.

senses.definition: To reduce the price of.
senses.example: They knocked it down by another £5, so we bought it.

senses.definition: To disassemble for shipment.
senses.example: The furniture is shipped knocked down, so assembly is required.

senses.definition: To acquire money, especially illicitly To embezzle.
senses.example: He was caught trying to knock down funds from the church's building account.

senses.definition: To accumulate money, usually through crime.
senses.example: The gang leader knocked down millions through gambling and extortion before the feds arrived.

senses.definition: To embezzle.
senses.example: The bookkeeper knocked down nearly two hundred thousand dollars before anyone noticed.

senses.definition: To drink or party To drink fast.
senses.example: I love to go down the pub and knock down pints of lager.

senses.definition: To drink fast.
senses.example: I love to go down the pub and knock down pints of lager.

senses.definition: To choose, declare or approve.
senses.example: The judge knocked the award down to a half-million.

senses.definition: To approve a drinking toast by banging glasses on the table.
senses.example: Before dinner, the guests knocked down their wine glasses to toast the new couple.

senses.definition: To reject or override a decision.
senses.example: The judge knocked the award down to a half-million.

senses.definition: To sentence (someone) to prison or other sentence.
senses.example: The judge knocked the defendant down to five years, angering the victim's family.

senses.definition: At an auction, to declare (something) sold with a blow from the gavel.
senses.example: The picture was knocked down for £50.

senses.definition: To sell.
senses.example: The dealer knocked the old Mustang down to a collector for twelve thousand dollars.

senses.definition: To reduce the burning of (a fire), as by cooling it with water or dirt.
senses.example: The crew knocked down the blaze with water and dirt before the fire spread.

senses.definition: (dated) To send a stop signal to ensure a train is signalled to stop at the correct point.
senses.example: In the 1920s, the signalman knocked down the distant signal so the express would stop.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To hit someone or something so that it falls to the ground, or to demolish a building; also to reduce a price.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on down, the particle, not on knock. In quick speech, the k of knock is silent and the two words link smoothly, sounding like nahk-DOWN.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. It can sound violent when it describes hitting a person, and it is usually plain and direct when describing buildings or prices.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say knock down a building or wall when it is demolished, and they say knock down the price in a negotiation, as in 'Can you knock down the price a little?' For a person hit by a car or a punch, use 'knocked down' in a factual report. For a more formal demolition, Americans say demolish or tear down.

distinctions.note: Knock down means to strike something so it falls or to demolish it, while knock off means to remove an amount or to stop working, so the meanings differ.
Demolish is more formal and suggests a planned, complete destruction of a structure, while knock down is more informal and can describe an accident or a quick action.

examples.everyday: The price was high, so I asked the guy at the flea market if he could knock it down a bit.
examples.professional: The crew will knock down the old warehouse next month to make room for the new office.
examples.analytical: To knock down an argument, you must identify its weakest premise rather than simply reject its conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Knocking something down is like pushing over a row of dominoes, where a single hit makes the whole thing fall.
nuance.etymology: From knock (Middle English knokken) and the adverb down, meaning to fall or cause to fall.
common_mistakes: Confusing knock down with knock off, which has separate meanings such as taking money off a price or copying a product.
Using knock down with a structure in a formal report where demolish is more natural.

senses.definition: A policy of governmental non-interference in economic affairs.
A policy of non-interference by authority in any competitive process.
senses.example: The senator defended a laissez faire approach, arguing that the market should be left alone.

senses.definition: Practicing or representing governmental noninterference, or minimal interference, especially in economic affairs; pertaining to free-market capitalism.
senses.example: I think the city should take a laissez faire approach to this; getting involved would only make things worse.

senses.definition: Advocating such noninterference.
senses.example: The Senator claims to be laissez faire, but he voted in favor of the subsidies.

senses.definition: Resulting from such noninterference.
senses.example: The price ceiling was well below the laissez faire price that demand would have supported, so there were always shortages.

senses.definition: Avoiding interference in other people's affairs; choosing to live and let live.
senses.example: My laissez faire manager lets the team decide their own schedules without any hovering.

core.definition: An economic policy in which the government does not interfere with markets or business, letting private decisions guide the economy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, FAIR, which is rhotic in American English. The first word is often said 'leh-zay,' not with the French vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in economics, but politically charged. Supporters see it as freedom; critics see it as neglect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use laissez-faire in economics, politics and business discussions, often about markets or regulation. In management, a laissez-faire leader is a hands-off boss who lets the team decide. Writing usually hyphenates it as laissez-faire when it is an adjective.

distinctions.note: A free market is an economic system; laissez-faire is the policy stance of government staying out of that system.
Hands-off is informal and everyday; laissez-faire is more formal and more often used for policy or leadership styles.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a real laissez-faire guy, so he thinks the government should just stay out of everything.
examples.professional: Our team lead took a laissez-faire approach, so we set our own sprint goals and only checked in once a week.
examples.analytical: Critics of laissez-faire economics argue that unregulated markets can produce monopolies that undermine the competition the policy is meant to protect.

nuance.analogy: Laissez-faire is like a referee who lets the players run the game, stepping in only when the rules are broken.
nuance.etymology: From French, meaning 'let [them] do' or 'allow to act.'
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the phrase with a French accent, as 'lay-ZAY fair'; Americans usually say 'leh-zay FAIR.'
Using laissez-faire as a noun for a relaxed person; it describes policies or styles, not people's personalities.

senses.definition: Brushing or flickering gently over a surface.
senses.example: Lambent candlelight flickered across the carved wooden pews as the choir began to sing.

senses.definition: Glowing or luminous, but lacking heat.
senses.example: The lambent glow of fireflies delighted the children.

senses.definition: Exhibiting lightness or brilliance of wit; clever or witty without unkindness.
senses.example: We appreciated her lambent comments.

core.definition: Softly glowing or flickering with light, or describing wit that is bright and lively without being cruel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle to a schwa, so it sounds like 'LAM-buhnt' with a short final T.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests gentle brilliance, whether of light or of wit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lambent' in literary writing, formal reviews and essays about style or light. It is rare in casual speech, so in conversation people say 'glowing' or 'witty' instead. Use it when you want to suggest soft, flickering brilliance.

distinctions.note: Luminous means emitting or full of light and is common, while lambent suggests a softer, flickering glow.
Radiant suggests strong shining or joy, while lambent suggests gentle, playful light or wit.

examples.everyday: Mom wrote in her card that the lake looked lambent at dusk, like it was glowing from underneath.
examples.professional: Her lambent humor kept the design review lively without ever turning cruel.
examples.analytical: The essay praises the author's lambent prose, where wit warms the reader without wounding anyone.

nuance.analogy: A lambent flame is like a candle flame in a draft, soft and flickering rather than fierce.
nuance.etymology: From Latin lambere, to lick or touch lightly.
common_mistakes: Using lambent for harsh or blazing light, when it means soft and flickering.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable.

senses.definition: One who has arrived comparatively recently.
senses.example: The old families in the neighborhood look down on him as a latecomer, his family only arrived in the 18th century, too nouveau for them.

senses.definition: One who arrived late.
senses.example: At the party the host made a point of greeting all the latecomers he missed in the first pass.

core.definition: A person who arrives after the scheduled start time or after most others have arrived.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LATE, the first part of the compound. The middle vowel is a short 'uh' as in 'come', and the final -er is a light American r-colored vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can sound mildly disapproving in a meeting, but it is often used lightly at parties or events.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use latecomer for people who show up after a meeting, party, or class has started. In a casual setting, you can say 'Save me a seat, I'm a latecomer.' A natural reply is 'Don't worry, you didn't miss much.' Be careful: a newcomer is someone new to a place or group, and that is a different meaning.

distinctions.note: A newcomer is someone new to a place, job, or group; a latecomer is someone who arrives after the scheduled time or after others.
A straggler lags behind a group, often on a walk or march; a latecomer arrives after the event begins.

examples.everyday: Save me a seat, I'm a latecomer to the potluck.
examples.professional: Latecomers to the call get the recording, but the big decisions were already made.
examples.analytical: As a latecomer to the debate, she had to answer objections the field had spent decades refining.

nuance.analogy: Like the last passenger who runs onto the train just as the doors are closing.
nuance.etymology: Compound of late and comer, from come (Old English cuman).
common_mistakes: Using latecomer for a new resident; say 'newcomer' when someone is new to a neighborhood or company.
Writing 'late comer' as two words; the standard form is 'latecomer'.

senses.definition: An imaginary line (in the form of a circumference) around a planet running parallel to the planet's equator.
senses.example: snow showers in the northerly latitudes

senses.definition: The relative freedom from restrictions; scope to do something.
senses.example: His parents gave him a great deal of latitude.

senses.definition: The extent to which a light-sensitive material can be over- or underexposed and still achieve an acceptable result.
senses.example: This film has enough latitude that slightly overexposed shots still look good.

senses.definition: Extent or scope; e.g. breadth, width or amplitude.
senses.example: The manager gave the team considerable latitude in choosing its own methods.

senses.definition: The angular distance north or south from a planet's equator, measured along the meridian of that particular point.
senses.example: The city sits at roughly forty degrees north latitude, so winters are cold.

senses.definition: The angular distance of a heavenly body from the ecliptic.
senses.example: Astronomers measured the comet's latitude relative to the ecliptic plane.

core.definition: The freedom or scope to make your own decisions and act without strict limits or constant supervision.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, LAT. The 'tude' ending is pronounced like 'tood', with a long oo sound, not 'tyood' as in British speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive, implying trust and freedom to act.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use latitude most often in workplace contexts, as in 'I have some latitude on this'. It is also common in discussions of law and policy. In geography, it refers to lines north or south of the equator, which is a separate sense you will hear in school and weather reports.

distinctions.note: Freedom is a broad, absolute concept, while latitude is a limited, granted range of choice within boundaries set by someone else.
Discretion emphasizes the authority to judge and decide, while latitude emphasizes the room to act within limits.

examples.everyday: My boss gives me a lot of latitude in how I schedule my week, which I really appreciate.
examples.professional: The team has latitude to choose its own tools, as long as the model meets our audit requirements.
examples.analytical: Judicial latitude in interpreting ambiguous statutes is constrained by the plain meaning of the text and by precedent.

nuance.analogy: Latitude is like the length of a leash: it lets you wander, but only within a certain range.
nuance.etymology: From Latin latitudo, breadth or width, from latus, wide.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final syllable with a British long u (tyood), which is less common in American speech.
Confusing latitude with longitude, which refers to east-west lines, not north-south ones.

latitude.etymology: Borrowed into Middle English from Old French *latitude*, from Latin *lātitūdō* (“breadth, width, latitude”), from *lātus* (“broad, wide”), from older *stlātus*.

senses.definition: A pit in which hides are stored.
The system of accepting a deposit and holding for a customer to complete a purchase.
senses.example: She put a winter coat on layaway so she could pay for it over the next two months.

senses.definition: An item which has been held in this way.

core.definition: A shopping system in which a store sets aside an item for you while you pay for it in installments, then you take it home after paying in full.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a weak, reduced 'uh.' Don't give the second syllable full stress or say it as two separate words, 'lay a way.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It suggests careful budgeting and patience, and some shoppers see it as a responsible alternative to credit card debt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use layaway mostly for big holiday gifts, furniture, or appliances, and many stores have reduced or ended these plans, so ask first whether the store still offers them. You usually say 'put it on layaway' or 'it's on layaway.' A natural reply when a clerk asks is 'Yes, I'd like to do layaway, please.'

distinctions.note: With an installment plan you take the goods home immediately and pay over time, while with layaway the store keeps the goods until you finish paying.
A credit card lets you borrow money to buy now, but layaway requires you to save money before you receive the item.

examples.everyday: I put the new crib on layaway at Target, and I'm paying twenty dollars a week until it's done.
examples.professional: Can you confirm whether the retailer still offers layaway on large appliances before we finalize the bulk order?
examples.analytical: Layaway shifts the risk of holding goods from the merchant to the customer, because the retailer keeps title to the item until final payment.

nuance.analogy: Like putting a coat on hold at the store and paying for it a little each paycheck until you can pick it up.
nuance.etymology: From the verb phrase 'lay away,' meaning to set aside or save for later.
common_mistakes: Using 'layaway' as a verb, as in 'I layaway the TV'; say 'I put the TV on layaway' instead.
Saying 'in layaway' instead of 'on layaway.'

conversation.text: My grandparents bought their first TV on layaway.
Do you still do layaway for the holidays?
I put the bike on layaway and paid for it over two months.

senses.definition: Layperson, someone who is not an ordained cleric or member of the clergy.
Someone who is not a professional in a given field.
senses.example: Carmen is not a professional anthropologist, but strictly a layman.

senses.definition: A common person.
A person who is untrained or lacks knowledge of a subject.
Lay-sister or lay-brother, person received into a convent of monks, following the vows, but not being member of the order.

core.definition: A person who is not an ordained member of the clergy, or someone who is not a professional or expert in a particular field.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the second syllable a weak 'uh' sound. Don't pronounce it as 'lay-MAN' with equal stress on both syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be respectful when it means a regular believer, but it can sound condescending when it implies someone lacks expertise.
nuance.usage_note: In church contexts Americans now usually say 'layperson' or 'laity,' because 'layman' refers to men only. In everyday speech, 'in layman's terms' is a common phrase for explaining something simply. Saying 'for a layman' can sound a bit condescending, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Layperson is gender-neutral and preferred in most American churches and professional settings, while layman refers to a man.
An expert has deep specialized knowledge, while a layman is simply someone outside that field, with no implied criticism of intelligence.

examples.everyday: I'm no mechanic, but in layman's terms, your car needs a new battery and an oil change.
examples.professional: I'll explain the security risk in layman's terms so the finance team can follow the decision.
examples.analytical: The Reformation emphasized that the layman shares in the priesthood of all believers, though the church has long distinguished ordained ministry from lay participation.

nuance.analogy: Like a passenger who enjoys the flight but does not know how the plane is flown.
nuance.etymology: From 'lay,' meaning people outside the clergy, from Middle English 'lay,' from Greek 'laikos,' of the people.
common_mistakes: Using 'layman' to refer to women, where 'layperson' or 'layman's terms' for general explanations is the normal choice.
Writing it as two words, 'lay man.'

layman.etymology: From Middle English *layman*, *lay man*, equivalent to *lay* + *man*.

senses.definition: The act of legislating; preparation and enactment of laws.
senses.example: pass legislation

senses.definition: A law which has been enacted by legislature or other governing body.
senses.example: The new legislation requires every restaurant to post calorie counts on menus.

core.definition: Laws passed by a legislature, or the process of making laws.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the syllable slay, and the ending -tion is pronounced shun. Do not pronounce the middle syllables as separate strong sounds; they are quick and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It refers to laws and lawmaking without emotional judgment, though specific pieces of legislation may be praised or criticized.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'legislation' in news, government, and business contexts, such as 'Congress passed new legislation on data privacy.' For one specific law, they often say 'a bill' before it is passed or 'a law' or 'a statute' after it is passed. In everyday talk, 'the new law' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Law is the general word for any rule that binds people, while legislation specifically means laws made by a legislature.
A statute is a single written law enacted by a legislature, while legislation can refer to one or many such laws together.
A regulation is a rule issued by an agency or government office, not by a legislature, although it may implement legislation.
A bill is a proposed law still being considered, while legislation usually refers to laws that have been passed.

examples.everyday: Did you hear about the new legislation on property taxes that passed last week?
examples.professional: Our compliance team has to update the data retention process to meet the new privacy legislation before July.
examples.analytical: Legislation is an imperfect instrument, since its wording always carries assumptions that courts must later interpret.

nuance.analogy: Legislation is like a building code: the legislature draws up the rules, and everyone who builds must follow them.
nuance.etymology: From Latin legis latio, 'proposal of a law', from lex, legis, 'law'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as lej-ih-SLAY-shun versus LEJ-ih-slay-shun; the stress is on slay.
Using legislation as a countable noun with a plural such as legislations in ordinary American writing.

legislation.etymology: From Late Latin *lēgislātiō* (“the giving of the law”).

senses.definition: A governmental body with the power to make, amend and repeal laws.
senses.example: state legislature

senses.definition: The legislative assembly of a province or territory, as opposed to the federal parliament.
senses.example: The provincial legislature in Ontario voted this week to expand funding for rural broadband projects.

senses.definition: A legislative building.

core.definition: An elected body of people with power to make, change, and repeal laws, such as a state legislature.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a secondary stress on slay, and the ending -ure is pronounced like 'cher' with an American r-colored vowel. Do not say the ending as 'chur' with a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a governmental institution and carries no praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, 'legislature' usually refers to a state's lawmaking body, such as the Texas legislature, while the federal body is called Congress. Americans often say 'the legislature' in news and everyday civic talk. A building where the body meets is usually called the statehouse or capitol.

distinctions.note: Congress is the national legislature of the United States, while legislature usually refers to a state body in American usage.
Parliament is the lawmaking body in countries such as the United Kingdom, and it is not the usual American term for a state or national body.
Legislation is the laws themselves, while legislature is the body that enacts them.

examples.everyday: The state legislature is meeting in Austin this week, so downtown traffic is terrible.
examples.professional: Our government affairs team tracks every bill that moves through the state legislature during this session.
examples.analytical: A legislature's power is not only to make laws but also to define the limits of executive discretion.

nuance.analogy: A legislature is like a company's board of directors: it sets the rules that the managers must follow.
nuance.etymology: Ultimately from Latin lex, 'law', through the word legislate.
common_mistakes: Using legislature for a single lawmaker; say legislator for one person.
Calling the U.S. federal body the legislature in casual speech; Americans usually say Congress.

core.definition: A female leopard.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, LEP. The final '-ess' is unstressed and sounds like 'iss', and the 'er' in the middle is a clear r-colored vowel, not a separate 'ur' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound elegant or poetic in literature, but it is not a charged word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans normally say 'female leopard' in everyday speech and in zoology. 'Leopardess' is an older, literary or occasional form, similar to 'lioness', and you will mainly see it in poetry, fiction or nature writing. Using it in casual conversation may sound a little formal, but it is not wrong.

distinctions.note: 'Female leopard' is the standard, neutral term in science and everyday speech, while 'leopardess' is more literary and less common.
'Lioness' is very common in American English, while 'leopardess' is rare, so the parallel can sound more deliberate or poetic.

examples.everyday: We saw a leopardess and her two cubs at the zoo this morning.
examples.professional: The conservation report tracked the leopardess and her cubs through two seasons of camera-trap data.
examples.analytical: The poet's image of the leopardess turns maternal protection into a kind of fierce, almost sacred hunting power.

nuance.analogy: A leopardess is to a leopard what a lioness is to a lion: the same animal, named by sex.
nuance.etymology: From 'leopard' (from Greek leopardos, 'lion-panther') plus the feminine suffix '-ess'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as 'ess' as in 'yes' rather than the reduced 'iss'.
Using 'leopardess' in everyday conversation where 'female leopard' is more natural.
Confusing 'leopardess' with 'leopardress', which is a spelling error.

senses.definition: A pause or period of slackening.
senses.example: without letup

core.definition: A pause or decrease in the intensity of something unpleasant, such as rain, noise, heat, or pressure.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, LET, and the second syllable is reduced to a weak 'up'. Do not stress the second syllable as in 'let-UP', which is the verb phrase.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly positive, because it usually signals relief from something difficult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'letup' mostly in the phrase 'no letup', as in 'no letup in the heat'. It is common in news and everyday speech. The verb is the two-word phrase 'let up', so you say 'the rain let up' but 'there was a letup in the rain'.

distinctions.note: A pause is a brief stop in an action or speech; a letup refers to a reduction in the intensity of an ongoing problem.
A break is a planned rest or interval; a letup is an unplanned easing of pressure or intensity.

examples.everyday: The rain finally showed a letup around noon, so we went to the park.
examples.professional: Support tickets have shown no letup since the release, so we need more staff on the weekend shift.
examples.analytical: The argument offers no letup from its central assumption, which it never tests.

nuance.analogy: A letup is like the lull in a storm, when the wind drops for a moment before it picks up again.
nuance.etymology: Noun formed from the phrasal verb 'let up', meaning to slacken or stop.
common_mistakes: Using 'letup' as a verb, as in 'the rain letup'; the verb is the two-word phrase 'let up'.
Writing 'let-up' or 'let up' as a noun, which are less common than 'letup' in American writing.

senses.definition: The quality, state or instance of being lewd; promiscuous.
senses.example: The film was rated for its lewdness, and the parents' group objected to several scenes.

core.definition: Sexual behavior or language that is offensive, crude or inappropriate in public settings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce it like 'lood', rhyming with 'food'. The final '-ness' is a reduced 'nus', not 'ness' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes moral disapproval of sexual behavior or sexualized conduct, often in legal or moralizing contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lewdness' in news reports, legal writing and moral criticism, such as 'charged with public lewdness.' It sounds stiff and judgmental in casual talk, so most people would say 'vulgar' or 'inappropriate' instead. Its use is more common in older or formal writing.

distinctions.note: Obscenity is a legal term for material considered offensive or illegal; lewdness is about conduct or behavior that is sexually suggestive in public.
Vulgarity refers to crude language or manners in general, while lewdness specifically concerns sexual suggestiveness.

examples.everyday: The comedian's jokes were so lewd that half the audience walked out.
examples.professional: The company's code of conduct forbids any lewdness in shared spaces, including online channels.
examples.analytical: Medieval moralists often confused lewdness with simple earthiness, which tells us as much about their categories as about the people they judged.

nuance.analogy: Lewdness is like a stain on a clean shirt: it draws the eye and breaks the expected standard of decency.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'læwed' (lay, unlearned), through the sense of coarse or ignorant, to sexual immorality.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'lewd' as 'lyoo-d' with a long u sound; it rhymes with 'food'.
Using 'lewdness' to describe mild humor; Americans reserve it for clearly sexual or indecent behavior.

senses.definition: An expert at lexicology.
senses.example: The lexicologist spent years tracing how words changed meaning across centuries.

core.definition: A scholar who studies words, including their meanings, internal structure and the relationships among them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAH, the cot vowel. The -ology part is reduced to luh-jist, so the middle syllables are quick and the end is -jist, not -gist.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a specialist and sounds scholarly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lexicologist mainly in linguistics departments, dictionaries and language research. It is uncommon in everyday talk, where people would say 'linguist' or 'language scholar.' Do not confuse it with lexicographer, the person who writes dictionaries.

distinctions.note: A lexicologist studies words theoretically, while a lexicographer compiles and writes dictionaries. Some people do both, but the roles differ.
A linguist studies language broadly, including sounds, grammar and history. A lexicologist focuses specifically on vocabulary and word structure.

examples.everyday: My friend is a lexicologist, so she gets excited when she hears a new slang word at dinner.
examples.professional: We hired a lexicologist to help us map the relationships between our product terms before we build the search index.
examples.analytical: A lexicologist would ask how a word's internal structure constrains the senses it can develop.

nuance.analogy: A lexicologist is like a botanist for words: they study the structure, growth and relationships of each word the way a botanist studies plants.
nuance.etymology: Formed from lexicology, from Greek lexikos 'of words' and -logia 'study of'.
common_mistakes: Confusing lexicologist with lexicographer, who writes dictionaries.
Stressing the -ol- syllable as LEK-sih-kahl-oj-ist, which shifts the rhythm.

lexicologist.etymology: From Ancient Greek *λεξικός* (“of words”), from *λέξις* (“a saying, speech, word”), from *λέγειν* (“to speak”).

senses.definition: An amount of money that is owed and has to be paid in the future, such as tax, debt, interest, and mortgage payments.
The right side of a balance sheet.
senses.example: The company's liabilities now exceed its assets, according to the latest balance sheet.

core.definition: Money or obligations that a person or company owes and must pay in the future, such as loans, bills, taxes and mortgage payments.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BIL, the third syllable of liability. The -ia- is reduced to uh, and the final -ities is pronounced ih-teez, with a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in finance, where it is a plain accounting term. In everyday speech, a single 'liability' can be negative, meaning someone or something that causes trouble.
nuance.usage_note: In American business, liabilities is the standard term on a balance sheet, opposite assets, and it covers debts and obligations. In everyday talk, people use the singular 'liability' informally for a person or thing that causes problems, as in 'He's a liability on the team.' Americans say 'debts' or 'what I owe' for personal money talk.

distinctions.note: Debts are specific amounts owed, such as a loan. Liabilities is the broader accounting category that includes debts and other obligations, such as accrued expenses.
Liabilities is the plural accounting term for what a company owes. The singular liability also means legal responsibility, such as product liability.

examples.everyday: Honestly, my car loan is one of my biggest financial liabilities right now.
examples.professional: Our balance sheet shows total liabilities of 4.2 million against 6 million in assets, so we are in good shape.
examples.analytical: Under accrual accounting, a liability is recognized when an obligation arises, not when the cash finally changes hands.

nuance.analogy: A balance sheet is like a personal money snapshot: assets are what you own, and liabilities are what you owe.
nuance.etymology: From liable, from Anglo-French liable 'bound by law,' from Latin ligare 'to bind.'
common_mistakes: Using the plural liabilities when speaking about one debt, where the singular liability is correct.
Thinking liabilities means only bank debt, when it also includes bills, taxes and other obligations.

senses.definition: A political party with libertarian values.

core.definition: A United States political party that favors limited government, low taxes, and maximum individual freedom in personal and economic matters.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAIR in libertarian and on PAR in party. In fast speech, the t in party is a flap, so it sounds like 'PAR-dee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in political conversation, but the label can be praised by supporters and criticized by opponents, so the tone depends on the speaker.
nuance.usage_note: Capitalize Libertarian Party when you mean the organization founded in 1971. Americans commonly say 'I'm a Libertarian' or 'I'm libertarian' to describe their views, but the lowercase word also refers to a broader political philosophy. Political discussions can get heated, so it helps to ask a question instead of arguing at once.

distinctions.note: The lowercase word can describe a philosophy or a person's views, while the Libertarian Party is the specific political organization.
Republicans generally support a larger role for government in some social and security matters. Libertarians emphasize personal freedom and smaller government more consistently.

examples.everyday: My neighbor always votes for the Libertarian Party because he wants less government in his life.
examples.professional: Our policy memo summarized the Libertarian Party platform on taxes and regulation for the client.
examples.analytical: The Libertarian Party platform rests on the premise that individuals should bear responsibility for their own choices within a minimal legal framework.

nuance.analogy: The party is like a referee who only blows the whistle for fouls, leaving the game itself to the players.
nuance.etymology: From libertarian, formed from liberty with a suffix for an adherent. The US party was founded in 1971.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying lib-er-TAR-ee-un instead of lib-er-TAIR-ee-un.
Using lowercase libertarian as if it were the name of the party, when the official name is capitalized.

senses.definition: A political philosophy maintaining that all persons are the absolute owners of their own lives, and should be free to do whatever they wish with their persons or property, provided they allow others that same liberty.
senses.example: Her libertarianism led her to oppose every law that told adults what they could do with their own property.

senses.definition: The doctrine of free will, as opposed to necessitarianism.
senses.example: In his philosophy seminar, we debated whether libertarianism could survive the claim that every event is causally determined.

core.definition: A political philosophy that favors maximum individual liberty, with minimal government interference in people's lives and property.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the -TAIR- syllable. The 'ee-uh-ni' syllables are weak, and the final -ism is a short 'izm'. Learners often stress the -ism syllable or drop the middle reduced syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to politically charged; supporters see it as a defense of freedom, critics as an attack on social protections.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'libertarianism' in political science, economics and public debates. It is most often associated with the Libertarian Party and thinkers who favor free markets and civil liberties. Saying 'I'm a libertarian' in conversation is common, and people usually expect a discussion about government size and personal freedom.

distinctions.note: Libertarian is the person or adjective; libertarianism is the philosophy itself.
In American usage, liberalism generally means a bigger role for government in social welfare; libertarianism generally means a smaller role.

examples.everyday: We argued about libertarianism over dinner, and I think we agreed more than we expected.
examples.professional: The policy memo summarizes the main arguments for and against libertarianism in digital privacy.
examples.analytical: Libertarianism rests on the claim that self-ownership grounds a strong presumption against coercion.

nuance.analogy: Libertarianism is like a fence drawn only around the things that must be protected, leaving the rest of the field open.
nuance.etymology: From 'libertarian' plus the suffix '-ism', from Latin 'libertas', freedom.
common_mistakes: Confusing libertarianism with libertinism, which refers to a lack of moral restraint.
Using it as an adjective; say 'libertarian ideas', not 'libertarianism ideas'.

senses.definition: A switch, usually mounted on a wall in a building, used to turn the light or another appliance such as a fan on and off.
senses.example: Please flip the light switch by the front door before you leave the room.

core.definition: A switch on a wall that turns a light or other electrical device on and off.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LITE, the first word of this compound noun. The t in light is clear, and the sw in switch is a smooth consonant cluster, so do not add a vowel between s and w.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical everyday word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use light switch for the wall control in homes and offices. You can say flip the light switch on or turn off the lights, and both are natural. For a switch that turns on a fan, Americans often use the term fan switch or wall control.

distinctions.note: A dimmer adjusts brightness gradually, while a light switch only turns the light on or off.

examples.everyday: Could you flip the light switch on the way out so the hallway isn't dark?
examples.professional: The electrician replaced the faulty light switch in the break room and checked the wiring.
examples.analytical: A light switch is a simple device, yet it depends on an entire network of wiring and safety rules.

nuance.analogy: Like a gate that opens or closes a path for electricity, a light switch decides whether the light flows.
nuance.etymology: Compound of light and switch, where switch comes from a term for a flexible rod or stick.
common_mistakes: Saying lamp switch for the wall control; a lamp switch is usually on the lamp itself.
Confusing switch with change in everyday speech; you turn the switch, not change it.

conversation.text: The light switch is on the left when you walk in.
I can't find the light switch in the dark.
This light switch controls the outlet by the couch.

senses.definition: Filled with light; illuminated.

core.definition: Filled with light or made bright, often by lamps, signs or fixtures, such as a lighted path or lighted sign.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LY, and the ending is pronounced 'id', like the sound in 'bit'. Speakers often mistakenly say 'LY-ted' because of the spelling.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, suggesting safety or welcome, as in a lighted entrance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lighted' mostly before a noun for things made bright by fixtures: a lighted sign, a lighted path, a lighted tennis court. For a room that is simply bright, people more often say 'well-lit' or 'lit up'. It is a neutral, fairly plain word, and no one would find it rude or dated.

distinctions.note: Lit is the past form of light and is used more in everyday speech, as in 'the room was lit'; lighted is more often placed before a noun.
Well-lit describes a place with good light, often in a safety or quality sense; lighted describes an object or area that has light fixtures.

examples.everyday: Stay on the lighted path back to the parking lot, because the other side is pretty dark.
examples.professional: The airport replaced the old runway signs with new LED fixtures so that the lighted edges are easier to see in fog.
examples.analytical: The painting shows a lighted window at dusk, and that single glowing point draws the eye to the solitary figure outside.

nuance.analogy: Like a porch light left on for a guest: it signals that the path is safe and someone is waiting.
nuance.etymology: From light (verb), from Old English lēoht; the -ed ending turned the participle into an adjective.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ending as 'ed' (rhymes with 'bed'); American speakers use 'id'.
Using 'lighted' for a person's face, as in 'his face was lighted'; that sounds old-fashioned, so say 'lit up' instead.

senses.definition: Given a subset S of a given topological space T, any point p whose every neighborhood contains some point, distinct from p, which belongs to S.
senses.example: In a metric space, every point of the closed interval is a limit point of the open interval.

core.definition: A point of a set S such that every neighborhood of it contains some point of S other than itself.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIM in the first word, and the second word's stress lands on POYNT. The reduced middle vowel in "limit" is a schwa-like sound, so say LIM-it, not LIM-ate.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is a precise term used in topology and real analysis, mainly in university courses and mathematical writing. Americans use it exactly as defined and do not use it in everyday speech. Be careful not to confuse it with the everyday word "limit," which means a boundary or maximum.

distinctions.note: In most modern texts the two terms are the same, but some authors reserve "accumulation point" for the same concept in metric spaces, so check the textbook's convention.
A limit of a sequence is a value the terms approach, while a limit point of a set is a point that other points of the set crowd around, which need not be a sequence limit.

collocations: every neighborhood contains a limit point
closed set contains all its limit points

examples.everyday: I didn't follow the lecture, but my roommate said the set's limit point is what makes the proof work.
examples.professional: Before we deploy the algorithm, we need to check whether the sequence of estimates has a limit point inside the feasible region.
examples.analytical: A set is closed precisely when it contains each of its limit points, so the boundary of an open ball is a closed set in any metric space.

nuance.analogy: Think of a crowd gathering around a single person: every small circle you draw around that person contains other people from the crowd.
nuance.etymology: "Limit" comes from Latin limes, limitem, meaning boundary; "point" comes from Latin punctum, meaning a prick or dot.
common_mistakes: Saying "limit point" with stress on the second word throughout, which makes it sound unnatural in American speech.
Assuming the point must belong to the set, when it need not.

senses.definition: Synonym of line graph.

core.definition: A graph that connects data points with straight line segments, usually to show how a value changes over time.

pronunciation.tip: LINE carries the main stress, and chart keeps a weaker secondary stress. Pronounce the r clearly, and use the open ah vowel of father in chart.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a plain, descriptive term for a common type of chart.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use line chart in business reports, software, and news graphics, and also in everyday talk about graphs on phones or fitness apps. In math classes and textbooks, the same thing is often called a line graph. Americans usually say chart for a visual of data, while graph in math and statistics can refer to a more specific structure.

distinctions.note: The two terms mean the same thing; line graph is more common in math and science classrooms, while line chart is more common in business and software.
A bar chart uses rectangular bars to compare separate categories. A line chart connects points to show change across an ordered sequence, such as time.
A scatter plot shows individual points without connecting them, so it shows relationships between variables. A line chart connects points in order.

collocations: a line chart of monthly sales
make a line chart in Excel

examples.everyday: My fitness app shows my weekly steps as a line chart, so I can see exactly when I slacked off.
examples.professional: I put the weekly churn rate on a line chart so the downward trend is obvious in the review meeting.
examples.analytical: A line chart suits this data because time is the ordered variable, so the slope between points shows the rate of change.

nuance.analogy: Like connecting dots on a map of your daily steps, so the path shows where you went up or down.
nuance.etymology: Line from Latin linea, meaning line; chart from Latin charta, meaning paper, through Old French.
common_mistakes: Giving both words equal stress; the first word carries the main stress.
Confusing a line chart with a trend line; the chart connects actual data points, while a trend line is a separate fitted line.

senses.definition: Pertaining to liturgy.
senses.example: The choir rehearsed liturgical music for the Easter service at the cathedral.

core.definition: Relating to the set forms and rituals of public Christian worship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: lih-TUR-jih-kul. The g sounds like j, and the r is rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; can be positive (rich, reverent) or negative (rigid, formal) depending on the speaker's church background.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it to describe churches with set orders of worship, such as Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, and Episcopal. People also say 'liturgical colors' or 'liturgical dance'. Non-liturgical churches usually avoid set forms.

distinctions.note: Ritual is general for any ceremonial act, while liturgical refers to formal worship.
Sacramental concerns the sacraments, whereas liturgical concerns the form of worship.
Ceremonial can apply to secular events, while liturgical is specifically religious.

examples.everyday: I grew up in a liturgical church, so a casual service feels unfamiliar.
examples.professional: The committee is reviewing the liturgical calendar for next year's services.
examples.analytical: A liturgical theology holds that worship forms belief as much as doctrine does.

nuance.analogy: Liturgical worship is like a script that a community performs together.
nuance.etymology: From Greek leitourgikos, relating to public service, from leitourgia.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the g as hard: 'lit-ur-GICK-al'.
Stressing the first syllable.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to movement or locomotion.
Something that is capable of locomotion.

core.definition: Relating to movement from one place to another, or to the body's ability to move.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MOH, the third syllable. The final -or is an unstressed, r-colored vowel that sounds like 'ter', not 'tor'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, technical word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: You will mostly meet this word in medicine, biology, physical therapy, and robotics. Americans would not use it in casual talk. In everyday speech they say 'movement' or 'mobility' instead. In clinical notes you might see 'locomotor skills' or 'locomotor function'.

distinctions.note: Locomotive usually means a railroad engine or, as an adjective, relating to movement. Locomotor is more clinical and refers to the body or animals moving.
Mobile is everyday and general, meaning able to move or easy to move. Locomotor is technical and tied to the act of locomotion.

examples.everyday: After his knee surgery, the physical therapist checked his locomotor skills before letting him walk to the car.
examples.professional: The robotics team tested the prototype's locomotor system on uneven terrain before the client demo.
examples.analytical: Early tetrapods show locomotor adaptations that allowed them to move on land while still keeping close ties to water.

nuance.analogy: Think of the locomotor system as the body's transportation network: the bones, muscles, and nerves that carry you from place to place.
nuance.etymology: From Latin locus, place, plus motor, mover, from movere, to move.
common_mistakes: Confusing locomotor with locomotive, which means a railroad engine.
Stressing the last syllable as 'loh-kuh-moh-TOR' instead of stressing the MOH syllable.

senses.definition: A feeling of depression resulting from being alone or from having no companions.
senses.example: The loneliness resulting from the loss of loved ones, lack of purpose in life, and social discrimination is a real inner hell.

senses.definition: The condition or state of being alone or having no companions.
The state of being unfrequented or devoid of human activity (of a place or time).

core.definition: A painful feeling of being alone or lacking companions, even when you are around other people at times.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, LONE. The final -ness is a quiet /nəs/ with a reduced vowel, not 'NESS'; keep the middle syllable short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names an unwelcome emotional state and usually signals sadness or isolation, so people often speak about it gently.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use loneliness for a personal feeling, often in conversations about health, aging, work, or moving to a new city. You can say 'I've been dealing with some loneliness since the move' to a friend. In casual talk, people often say 'I've been feeling lonely' instead, which sounds more natural than naming the noun.

distinctions.note: Solitude is chosen and can feel peaceful, while loneliness is an unwelcome feeling of disconnection.
Isolation describes an external situation of being cut off from people, while loneliness is the inner feeling, which can happen even in a crowd.

examples.everyday: Since her kids moved out, she's been struggling with a lot of loneliness, so she joined a book club.
examples.professional: Our remote team survey showed that loneliness was a bigger factor in turnover than we had expected.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard distinguishes solitude that enriches the self from a loneliness that arises when the self loses its relation to others and to God.
