It appears mainly in formal, legal, historical or academic writing. In conversation, 'misinformer' is a near equivalent, though it is also uncommon.

distinctions.note: An informant gives information, which may be accurate, while a misinformant gives wrong information.
A liar knowingly says false things; a misinformant may simply be wrong, so the term does not require intent.
Misinformer is a close synonym and slightly more common in general writing.

examples.professional: The source turned out to be a misinformant, so we removed his claims from the incident report.
examples.analytical: Historians distinguish the deliberate liar from the honest misinformant who repeats an error in good faith.

nuance.analogy: Like a GPS that confidently gives wrong turns; it is trusted, but it leads you astray.
nuance.etymology: From mis- (wrongly) and informant (one who informs), from Latin informare.
common_mistakes: Using misinformant as a verb.
Confusing it with 'informant' and assuming it is always a positive term.

senses.definition: Having two or more separate aspects.
senses.example: I get a very mixed feeling from this puzzling painting.

senses.definition: Not completely pure, tainted or adulterated.
senses.example: My joy was somewhat mixed when my partner said she was pregnant: it's a lot of responsibility.

senses.definition: Including both male(s) and female(s).
senses.example: The tennis match was mixed, with a boy and a girl on each side.

senses.definition: Stemming from two or more races or breeds.
senses.example: The benefit dog show has both mixed and single-breed competitions.

senses.definition: Polarizing; including both positive and negative feedback.
senses.example: The movie has received mixed reviews from movie critics.

core.definition: Made of or including different kinds of things, or having both good and bad parts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable. The -ed ending is not a separate syllable, and it sounds like a t after the k, so the word ends with a quiet st.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. Mixed often signals a result that is neither clearly good nor clearly bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say mixed reviews, mixed feelings, mixed nuts and mixed results all the time. The word also appears in mixed martial arts and mixed company. In casual speech it often means not all good, which is a polite way to say something was disappointing.

distinctions.note: Mixed means combined or varied, while mixed-up means confused or muddled in the mind.
Varied means different from each other, while mixed suggests things that have been combined together.

examples.everyday: I got mixed reviews from my friends about the new movie.
examples.professional: The pilot program had mixed results, with strong engagement but weak conversion.
examples.analytical: His mixed record makes it hard to judge whether the policy failed or succeeded only in some places.

nuance.analogy: Mixed is like a fruit salad: many good pieces together, but not all of them taste the same.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of mix, from Middle English mixen.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ed as a separate syllable, as in MIKS-ed.
Using mixed to mean confused, which is mixed-up in American English.

senses.definition: Comprising both males and females.
senses.example: a mixed-sex school

core.definition: Including both males and females together, such as a team, school, group or living space.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second part, sex. Keep the final t of mixed short, and say the k clearly before the s in sex.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise descriptive term, sometimes used in formal documents or policy discussions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say coed for schools and sports leagues, or mixed-gender in policy and research writing. Mixed-sex is used in formal or technical contexts, such as medical forms or reports on residency programs. In casual speech it can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Coed is common and informal in American English for schools, teams and dorms, while mixed-sex sounds more formal and descriptive.
Mixed-gender stresses social roles and identity, while mixed-sex focuses on biological or categorical sex.

examples.everyday: Our rec volleyball team is mixed-sex, so we have men and women playing together.
examples.professional: The hospital's residency program is mixed-sex, and HR reviews representation in each cohort.
examples.analytical: Studies of mixed-sex groups show that gendered norms can shape who speaks first and who gets interrupted.

nuance.analogy: A mixed-sex team is like a band with different voices singing together, each part adding to the sound.
nuance.etymology: Mixed from mix; sex from Latin sexus.
common_mistakes: Writing mixed sex without the hyphen when it comes before a noun.
Using mixed-sex in casual speech where Americans would say coed or just mixed.

senses.definition: An organization's processes for approving, documenting, monitoring and retiring models.
senses.example: Our bank's model governance team reviews every credit-scoring model before it goes live.

core.definition: An organization's processes for approving, documenting, monitoring, validating and retiring machine learning models throughout their lifecycle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GUV in 'governance', and the 'ern' syllable is a reduced vowel that sounds like 'ur'. Many learners add a full vowel to 'gov' and say 'GOH-vern-ance'; in American speech it is short and reduced, with a silent e in effect. The final syllable is 'nuns', not 'nance'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, because it signals control, accountability and responsible practice.
nuance.usage_note: Banks, insurers and large tech companies use this term when they discuss regulatory compliance and risk management for AI systems. In meetings, people often say 'our model governance framework' or 'the model governance committee.' It sounds formal, so casual conversations usually use simpler words like 'oversight.'

distinctions.note: Model risk management focuses on the risk of model errors, while model governance covers the broader processes and accountability structure.
Oversight is a general word for supervision, while governance is a more formal, structured system of rules and responsibilities.

examples.everyday: My brother works at a bank and says they spend a lot of time on model governance because regulators check everything.
examples.professional: Before we deploy this credit model, we need sign-off from the model governance team and an updated validation report.
examples.analytical: Model governance can be understood as the institutional response to the epistemic opacity of machine learning, since it distributes accountability across people and procedures.

nuance.analogy: Model governance is like a building inspection system: it checks the plans, monitors the structure over time, and decides when a building must be retired.
nuance.etymology: 'Govern' comes from Latin gubernare, to steer or pilot a ship; 'governance' is the act or manner of governing.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'governance' with a full vowel in the middle syllable instead of a reduced 'ur' sound.
Using 'governance' as a synonym for 'government' in general; here it refers to organizational processes, not a state.

conversation.text: Model governance covers how models are approved, documented, monitored, and retired.
Banks have long had model governance requirements for credit and risk models.
Good model governance means we can say exactly which model version made each decision.

senses.definition: The state or degree of being moldy.
senses.example: The moldiness of the bread meant that it was unpalatable, if not downright inedible.

core.definition: The state of being covered with mold, or the musty, decayed smell and look that mold causes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is short 'dee' and the final '-ness' is reduced to 'nus.' Avoid stressing the second syllable, which is a common error for words ending in '-iness.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something unpleasant, unhealthy, or dirty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'moldiness' in everyday speech about rooms, food, bread, bathrooms, and basements, often with a complaint: 'I smell the moldiness in the carpet.' It is a less common word than 'mold' or 'moldy,' so people usually say 'the mold' or 'it's moldy' in casual conversation. The spelling is 'moldiness' in American English.

distinctions.note: 'Mustiness' describes a stale, damp smell, often without visible mold; 'moldiness' refers more directly to the mold growth itself.
'Rot' refers to organic decay in general; 'moldiness' specifically describes mold growth.

examples.everyday: I can't stand the moldiness in this bathroom, so I'm calling the landlord today.
examples.professional: The inspection report noted visible moldiness on the north wall, which needs remediation before occupancy.
examples.analytical: The novel uses moldiness as a symbol of a marriage that has gone stale, unnoticed until the smell is unavoidable.

nuance.analogy: Moldiness is like a forgotten sponge left in a closed bucket: it looks dark, smells sour, and tells you something has been growing where no one was looking.
nuance.etymology: From mold (Middle English mould, from Old English molde, 'earth, soil') plus the suffixes -y and -ness; the sense of fungus developed later.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying 'mol-DEE-ness.'
Using 'moldiness' when 'mold' is the more natural noun in casual talk.

senses.definition: The property of being momentary.
senses.example: The momentariness of the flash made it hard to photograph the lightning.

core.definition: The quality of lasting only a moment; the brief, passing nature of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MOH-, and give a secondary stress to -tair-. The middle syllables are weak, so say 'mun' rather than 'men'. The word ends in a soft -nus, not -ness with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a feature of time or experience without judging it, though it can carry a wistful tone when applied to beauty or joy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in everyday speech; they say 'how brief it was' or 'it lasted only a moment' instead. You will meet it in philosophy, literature, and academic writing about experience or time. In casual talk, 'brevity' or 'briefness' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Transience stresses that things pass away and do not last, often with a sense of loss; momentariness emphasizes the very short duration itself.
Brevity is common and general, describing short length of anything, including writing; momentariness is a formal word about how long a state or experience lasts.

examples.professional: The glitch is hard to reproduce because the momentariness of the spike leaves almost no trace in our logs.
examples.analytical: Some phenomenologists argue that the momentariness of conscious experience resists any single description, since each present moment already slips into the past.

nuance.analogy: Like a camera flash: the light is intense and real, but it exists only for an instant.
nuance.etymology: From momentary plus -ness; momentary comes from Late Latin momentaneus, from Latin momentum 'movement, moment'.
common_mistakes: Using momentariness in casual speech where brevity or 'how short it was' is more natural.
Confusing momentarily, which in American English can mean 'for a short time' or 'in a moment', with the noun momentariness.

senses.definition: The property of being monolithic.

core.definition: The quality of being monolithic, meaning unified and uniform as one undivided whole without internal variation.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the 'SIS' syllable of '-icity', and the final '-ity' is a light 'ih-tee'. Learners often stress the 'lith' syllable or pronounce the 'c' as 'k', but here it is a soft 's' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it often describes a structure or group in a critical way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use monolithicity in academic writing, political science, and systems design, usually when a critic wants to argue that a group, institution, or code base is less varied than it appears. It is rare in everyday speech, and many Americans would just say 'how uniform it is' or 'how much it acts as one'. It is a heavy word, so use it only in formal or analytical contexts.

distinctions.note: Uniformity refers to sameness among parts, while monolithicity describes a single, indivisible whole.
Cohesion is a positive term for things holding together well, while monolithicity can suggest a lack of flexibility or diversity.

examples.professional: The audit found that the codebase's monolithicity made it hard to test any single module in isolation.
examples.analytical: The historian challenges the monolithicity often attributed to medieval guilds, showing their internal rivalries and divisions.

nuance.analogy: Monolithicity is like a single cast bell that rings as one piece, compared with a mosaic made of many separate tiles.
nuance.etymology: From monolithic, from Greek monolithos 'of one stone', with the noun ending -icity.
common_mistakes: Using monolithicity to describe a physical object; it describes a quality, and the object is a monolith.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the 'SIS' syllable.
Confusing it with monolith, which is the noun for the thing itself.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being monstrous.
Something monstrous.

core.definition: The quality of being shockingly cruel, ugly, or extreme; the horror of something monstrous.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MAHN. The ending -ness is short and unstressed, so say 'nus' with a reduced vowel, and avoid adding an extra syllable in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a quality of extreme cruelty, horror, or ugliness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use monstrousness in everyday talk. They prefer monstrosity for a specific thing or cruelty or horror for a moral quality. It appears most often in essays, commentary, criticism, or serious discussion of crimes and injustice.

distinctions.note: Monstrosity usually names a concrete ugly thing or act; monstrousness names the underlying quality of being monstrous.
Cruelty is a general word for causing pain; monstrousness suggests an extreme, shocking degree of cruelty or horror.
Horror is an emotional reaction or the thing that causes it; monstrousness describes the quality that provokes horror.

examples.professional: The monstrousness of the outage was that it wiped out the backups along with the primary database.
examples.analytical: The monstrousness of the crime lies less in its violence than in its calm, bureaucratic routine.

nuance.analogy: Like the deep darkness under a calm lake: the surface looks ordinary, but the quality of what lies below is what alarms you.
nuance.etymology: From monstrous, from Latin monstrum, plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using it for a concrete object; say monstrosity for a building or product.
Confusing it with monster, which names a being rather than a quality.

senses.definition: An inner sense that distinguishes right from wrong, functioning as a guide for morally appropriate behavior.
A belief system, person, etc. serving as a guide for morally appropriate behavior.
senses.example: Her grandmother's faith remained her moral compass through every difficult decision in life.

core.definition: An inner sense of right and wrong that guides a person's choices, or a person, belief or principle that serves that guiding role.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of each word, with moral's stress slightly weaker than compass's. The second syllable of moral is a reduced schwa, and compass is pronounced with a short u as in cup.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a person for having reliable ethical judgment, though people can say someone has lost their moral compass to criticize bad behavior.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use moral compass often in news, speeches, sermons and everyday talk about character, as in she has a strong moral compass. Saying someone has lost their moral compass is a common and fairly strong criticism. A natural reply is something like I agree, he always seemed to do the right thing before.

distinctions.note: Conscience is the feeling of guilt or approval about one's own actions, while moral compass is a broader guide for decisions across many situations.
Ethics refers to the systematic study or code of right conduct, while moral compass refers to a personal or institutional sense of direction.

examples.everyday: My grandmother had a strong moral compass, and she never let us cut corners, even when nobody was watching.
examples.professional: Our leadership training stresses a moral compass that guides decisions when the policy does not cover the situation.
examples.analytical: A moral compass, unlike a rulebook, orients the agent toward right action in situations no code anticipated.

nuance.analogy: A moral compass works like a magnetic needle: it does not tell you the whole route, but it keeps pointing you back toward north when the terrain is confusing.
nuance.etymology: Moral comes from Latin moralis, relating to manners or customs; compass comes from Old French compas, a circle or measure.
common_mistakes: Using moral compass for a set of formal rules, when it refers to an inner or guiding sense of right and wrong.
Stressing compass on the second syllable, which is wrong; the stress falls on the first syllable.

moral-compass.etymology: From *moral* + *compass*, from the fact that a compass indicates various directions on its face (sense 3), and enables its user to find the correct direction to go in (sense 1).

senses.definition: Of or relating to those mental images that arise from the sensations of bodily movement and position.
senses.example: The psychologist asked whether her mental images were motile, arising from feelings of movement rather than sight.

senses.definition: In organisms: having the power to move spontaneously.
senses.example: Biologists observed that the larval stage of the parasite is motile, swimming freely through the water.

senses.definition: In organs or organelles: capable of producing motion.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the motile cilia of the cells beat rhythmically to clear mucus.

senses.definition: In organs: having the power to move their contents, or to change their shape or tension by writhing or contracting as required by their particular physiological functions.
senses.example: The motile stomach muscles contract in waves to push food through the digestive tract.

senses.definition: A person whose prevailing mental imagery takes the form of inner feelings of action, such as incipient pronunciation of words, muscular innervations, etc.
senses.example: In the psychology lab, she turned out to be a motile, silently rehearsing each word she saw.

core.definition: Able to move on its own, without outside force, used in biology for living cells and organisms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, MOH, and the second syllable is a reduced 'tuhl'. Non-native speakers often give the second syllable a full 'eel' vowel or stress it, which makes the word sound like a different word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a precise scientific term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use motile in biology, microbiology, and medicine to describe cells, sperm, or bacteria that can move on their own. In everyday speech they say moving or mobile instead. The noun sense in the input comes from psychology about imagery and is rarely used now.

distinctions.note: Mobile means able to be moved or to move around easily in everyday life, while motile is a technical term for spontaneous movement by a living organism.
Motor refers to a machine or a neural pathway, while motile describes the ability of a living thing to move itself.

examples.everyday: My biology roommate said the bacteria in the sample are motile, so they swim around in the dish.
examples.professional: Our lab report notes that only the motile cells in the sample showed a response to the drug.
examples.analytical: The distinction between motile and sessile organisms raises the question of how agency is defined in living systems.

nuance.analogy: A motile cell is like a tiny swimmer with its own engine, while a sessile cell is like a plant rooted in one spot.
nuance.etymology: From Latin motus, meaning moved, plus the suffix -ile, able to.
common_mistakes: Confusing motile with mobile in everyday contexts.
Using the rare psychological noun sense in ordinary conversation.

motile.etymology: From Latin *mōtus*, perfect passive participle of *moveō* (“to move”), *ile*.

senses.definition: Someone who has power and influence in a field or activity; one who accomplishes tasks, who gets things done.
senses.example: The sales team sought to talk to the movers and shakers within an organization, rather than to their underlings.

core.definition: A person with power and influence in a field who gets important things done and drives change.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SHAY in shaker, and the middle word is reduced to a weak uhnd, so do not say a full 'and'. Keep the first syllable of mover strong and slide quickly into the unstressed -er.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises someone for energy and influence. It can sound slightly flattering or jokey, so use it with warmth rather than in formal reports.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in news stories, business talk and small talk about local leaders, as in 'She's a mover and shaker in city politics.' It is often plural in general statements, as in 'the movers and shakers of Silicon Valley.' A natural reply is 'Oh, really?' or 'She sounds like someone who gets things done.'

distinctions.note: A leader usually holds a formal role, while a mover and shaker can have influence without any official title.
Big shot is more informal and can sound slightly sarcastic, while mover and shaker is usually admiring.

collocations: a mover and shaker in local politics
the movers and shakers of Silicon Valley

examples.everyday: My neighbor Linda is a real mover and shaker, so she knows everyone who matters at the city council meetings.
examples.professional: Our VP of Product is the real mover and shaker here, so get her buy-in before you pitch the new dashboard.
examples.analytical: Historians often focus on the movers and shakers of an era, but the quiet organizers beneath them shaped its outcomes just as much.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone thrown into still water, a mover and shaker sends ripples through the whole group.
nuance.etymology: Mover comes from Middle English move (Old French mover, Latin movere, 'to move'); shaker comes from Old English sceacan, 'to shake'.
common_mistakes: Using it for a physical mover; the phrase is figurative and refers only to influence.
Pronouncing the middle 'and' fully, which sounds stiff; say it as uhnd.

senses.definition: The characteristics of an organization, society, city etc. which has many different ethnic or national cultures mingling freely; political or social policies which support or encourage such coexistence.
senses.example: Chicago's multiculturalism is visible in its neighborhoods, restaurants, and festivals.

senses.definition: The cultural Marxism conspiracy theory.
senses.example: Some online extremists blame multiculturalism on a fictional cultural Marxism plot.

core.definition: The presence of many cultures living together in one society, along with policies that support their coexistence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KUHL, and the -ism ending is a weak 'um'. The middle syllable 'chur' is a rhotic reduced vowel, so do not stress it. Say the word with a smooth, unbroken rhythm.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing diversity, but it is a contested political term and can be used critically.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use multiculturalism in discussions of society, education, politics, and public policy. It can sound positive when praising a diverse community, but critics also use it to argue about assimilation or group identity. In casual conversation people usually prefer diversity or a multicultural city, but the noun is common in news and academic writing.

distinctions.note: Diversity describes variety in general, including race, gender, and ideas. Multiculturalism refers specifically to cultures coexisting and often to policies that support them.
Assimilation means minority groups adopting the dominant culture. Multiculturalism emphasizes that several cultures can keep their distinct identities within one society.

examples.everyday: Living in Queens really shows you what multiculturalism looks like, with people from everywhere on the same subway.
examples.professional: Our company's policy on multiculturalism covers hiring, language access, and the holiday calendar.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that multiculturalism can emphasize group identity at the expense of individual rights and shared citizenship.

nuance.analogy: Like a symphony where many instruments play different parts, and the music is richer because each one keeps its own sound.
nuance.etymology: From multicultural (from multi- plus cultural) plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for diversity in every sense; it refers specifically to cultures and policies.
Pronouncing the middle syllables with full vowels, as in 'mul-tee-KUHL-chur-AL-iz-um'.

senses.definition: The combined use of sound, video, and text to present an idea.
Of, or relating to this combined use of media.
senses.example: The museum's multimedia exhibit combines video, sound, and interactive touchscreens.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to an application that can combine such media into an integrated package.
senses.example: The new software is multimedia, letting users edit photos, audio, and video together.

core.definition: Content or presentations that combine text, sound, images and video; also used as an adjective.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MEE, the second syllable of 'media', and the final syllable is a light schwa, 'uh', not 'ah'. Americans say the first part of media as 'MEE' in standard speech, though 'MED' is also heard.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a format or method, and it is often used in marketing, education and technology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'multimedia' for presentations, lessons, apps and messages that mix formats, such as 'a multimedia presentation' or 'multimedia content.' The noun is used as a mass noun, so you say 'multimedia' without 'a' unless you mean a particular example. The word was a buzzword in the 1990s and is now more common in education, marketing and phone messaging.

distinctions.note: Mixed media is an art term for a single artwork made from different materials, while multimedia refers to digital or presentation formats.
Multimedia describes the formats delivered to people; multimodal describes communication or data using several modes, including in AI and linguistics.
Hypermedia is multimedia linked by hyperlinks, so the user moves between items; the term is more technical and less common in daily speech.

examples.everyday: My nephew sent me a multimedia message with a video and a few photos from his trip.
examples.professional: For the onboarding session, I'd like to build a short multimedia presentation with narration, a demo video and a slide deck.
examples.analytical: Multimedia communication challenges the assumption that a message is judged by its words alone, because meaning emerges from sound and image together.

nuance.analogy: Like a meal served on one plate, where text, sound and images arrive together instead of in separate courses.
nuance.etymology: Multi- from Latin multus 'many', plus media, the plural of medium, from Latin medium 'middle, intermediate'.
common_mistakes: Using multimedia as a countable noun, as in 'a multimedia' for one item; say 'a multimedia presentation' or 'multimedia content'.
Confusing it with mixed media, which is a term in art rather than digital presentation.

senses.definition: Persistently annoying or painful.
senses.example: nagging doubt

senses.definition: Causing persistent mild pain, or annoyance.
The action of the verb nag.
senses.example: Her constant nagging about the dishes finally got him to start loading the dishwasher.

core.definition: Persistently annoying, or causing a dull, lingering pain, worry or doubt that does not go away.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, NAG, and the final -ing is a short, reduced ih sound, not a long ee. Keep the g hard, and do not let the ng become n followed by g.

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it describes something that keeps bothering or worrying someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nagging in two common ways: for a persistent pain, such as a nagging backache, and for a lingering feeling, such as a nagging doubt or sense that something is forgotten. It is neutral to informal and sounds natural in everyday speech and writing. In the sense of a person who keeps complaining, nagging is a noun or adjective, but the adjective sense is more common in daily American English.

distinctions.note: Persistent is neutral and can describe anything that continues, while nagging suggests something annoying or worrying that keeps coming back.
Chronic is a medical or formal term for a long-lasting condition, while nagging describes a small but irritating pain or feeling.

examples.everyday: I have a nagging feeling that I left the stove on, so I am going to drive back and check.
examples.professional: There is a nagging concern about the data pipeline, so I want to double-check the logs before the release.
examples.analytical: A nagging question remains: if the argument depends on an unexamined premise, how far does its conclusion really reach?

nuance.analogy: A nagging doubt is like a pebble in your shoe: small enough to ignore for a moment, but it keeps reminding you with every step.
common_mistakes: Using nagging with a person as its subject when you mean the feeling or pain; say a nagging doubt, not a nagging person, unless you mean an annoying person.
Pronouncing the ing as a long ee sound.

senses.definition: The religion of the Nazarenes.

core.definition: The faith, doctrine, or practice of the Nazarenes, including early Jewish-Christian groups and, in modern usage, the Church of the Nazarene.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on REEN, the third syllable, and the final -ism is a reduced unstressed syllable. Do not confuse it with Nazism, which is a different word with a different stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term in religious studies and church history, with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use Nazarenism in ordinary conversation. It appears in academic writing on early Christianity and in discussions of the Church of the Nazarene, a Protestant holiness denomination. Capitalize Nazarene when referring to people or the church, and keep the lowercase form only in quoted historical contexts.

distinctions.note: A Nazarene is a person who follows the faith, while Nazarenism is the system of belief or the movement itself.
Nazism is a political ideology from twentieth-century Germany and is completely unrelated to Nazarenism, though the spelling is close.
A Nazirite is a person under a special vow in Numbers 6, whereas Nazarenism is a religious movement or identity.

examples.professional: Her seminar paper compared early Nazarenism with other Jewish-Christian movements in the first century.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether Nazarenism was a distinct sect or a Jewish-Christian tendency within the wider early church.

nuance.analogy: Nazarenism is to a Nazarene what Methodism is to a Methodist: the system of belief behind the believers.
nuance.etymology: From Nazarene, from Greek Nazōraios, from Nazareth, the town of Jesus' upbringing.
common_mistakes: Confusing Nazarenism with Nazism because the spellings are similar.
Using lowercase nazarene in modern contexts where Americans capitalize the church name.
nuance.biblical_note: Nazarene in the New Testament is a name for Jesus and his followers, connected to the town of Nazareth. Matthew 2:23 describes Jesus going to live in Nazareth so that the prophets would be fulfilled, using the title 'He shall be called a Nazarene.' Acts 24:5 refers to the Nazarenes as a sect, showing that the name was already used for followers of Jesus. The Greek word is Nazōraios (Ναζωραῖος), linked to Nazareth, and Mark 1:24 uses the phrase Jesus of Nazareth.

senses.definition: Myopic, suffering from myopia.
senses.example: Because she was near-sighted, she sat in the front row to read the board.

core.definition: Able to see close objects clearly but unable to see distant objects clearly without glasses or contact lenses; nearsighted.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on NEAR, the first syllable, and the second part sounds like sight. The ending -ed is a short unstressed id, not a separate ay sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a common vision condition, though people sometimes joke about it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use nearsighted for vision, as in I'm nearsighted, so I need glasses to drive. Eye doctors and medical texts prefer myopic or myopia. Figurative use is less common than shortsighted, which describes a lack of planning or foresight in business or politics.

distinctions.note: Farsighted is the opposite: a person sees distant objects clearly but has trouble with close ones.
Myopic is more technical and medical, and it is also used figuratively for shortsighted thinking.
Shortsighted usually describes poor planning or judgment, while nearsighted is literal and refers to eyesight.

examples.everyday: I'm pretty nearsighted, so I can't read road signs at night without my glasses.
examples.professional: Our reporting is too nearsighted, since the dashboard shows only last week's numbers and misses the longer trend.
examples.analytical: A nearsighted strategy optimizes for immediate results and neglects consequences that appear only years later.

nuance.analogy: Being nearsighted is like having a camera that focuses beautifully up close but blurs the horizon.
nuance.etymology: A compound of near and sighted, from Old English gesiht 'sight'.
common_mistakes: Saying nearsighted for distant objects when the meaning is reversed; a nearsighted person sees near things well.
Stressing the second syllable, saying near-SIGHT-ed, instead of the usual NEAR-sight-ed pattern.

senses.definition: A method that predicts using the most similar training examples (k-nearest neighbors).
senses.example: For the recommendation model, we used nearest neighbor with k set to five to find similar customers.

core.definition: A method that predicts a new item's label or value using the most similar examples in its training data, usually the k closest ones.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on NAY in 'neighbor', with a lighter stress on 'NEER' in 'nearest'. The final -or is a reduced American 'er', not 'or'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and engineers say 'nearest neighbor' or 'k-nearest neighbors' (kNN) in technical talk, and often just 'kNN'. Outside technical settings the phrase means a literal neighbor. In meetings, say 'we used nearest neighbor' to name the method, and describe it as instance-based because it stores data rather than learning a fixed model.

distinctions.note: k-means is unsupervised clustering that groups data; nearest neighbor is a supervised method that predicts labels for new points.
In ordinary speech a neighbor is a person living nearby; in machine learning it is a stored training example.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is the nearest neighbor I could ask about the parking rules.
examples.professional: For this prototype, let's start with nearest neighbor since it needs no training step.
examples.analytical: Nearest neighbor methods are non-parametric, so their predictions depend directly on the stored examples and the chosen distance metric.

nuance.analogy: Like asking the few people who look most like you what they chose, and going with their majority.
nuance.etymology: Nearest from Old English nēahst, and neighbor from Old English nēahgebūr, 'near dweller'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'neighbour' with British spelling; use neighbor.
Stressing 'NEAR-est' too strongly, which weakens the natural rhythm.

conversation.text: A nearest neighbor classifier assigns the label of the closest training example.
Approximate nearest neighbor search makes embedding lookup fast across millions of vectors.

senses.definition: The drink of the gods.
Any delicious drink, now especially a type of sweetened fruit juice.
The sweet liquid secreted by flowers to attract pollinating insects and birds.
To feed on nectar.
senses.example: Nectaring is one of butterflies' favorite activities.

core.definition: A sweet, delicious liquid, such as fruit juice or a sugary drink; also the sugary liquid flowers make to attract bees and birds.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. In General American the middle t between vowels is a quick flap, close to a 'd' sound, and the final syllable is a reduced 'er', not 'ar'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests something sweet, rich and pleasant, and in literature it can mean a divine or heavenly drink.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nectar in everyday talk to praise a sweet drink or delicious fruit, as in 'this peach is pure nectar.' For ordinary juice people say juice, and for flowers they say nectar in science or gardening talk. Using it for drinks can sound a little poetic, so people often say it with a smile.

distinctions.note: Juice is the ordinary word for fruit liquid; in the US, nectar usually means a thicker, sweetened fruit drink, and it sounds more appealing.
Honey is made by bees from nectar; nectar is the raw sugary liquid in flowers, while honey is the processed product.

examples.everyday: Those fresh peaches you brought are pure nectar, thanks so much for bringing them over!
examples.professional: Our new beverage line uses peach nectar as the base, so we have to check the sugar levels against the labeling rules before launch.
examples.analytical: The ancient poets imagined nectar as the drink of the gods, a sign that the divine was sweet, immortal and unlike anything humans could taste.

nuance.analogy: Nectar works like a tip jar at a bakery: a small sweet reward that brings visitors back.
nuance.etymology: From Greek nektar, the drink of the gods.
common_mistakes: Saying NEK-tar with a broad a; the final syllable is a reduced 'er' sound.
Using nectar for ordinary juice in everyday talk; it sounds intentionally poetic.

nectar.etymology: From Latin *nectar*, from Ancient Greek *νέκταρ* (“nourishment of the gods”), from Proto-Indo-European **neḱ-* (“perish, disappear”) +, from **terh₂-* (“to overcome, pass through, cross over”).

senses.definition: In a needless manner.
To a degree or extent beyond what is needed.
senses.example: He was always needlessly anxious about his dog.

senses.definition: Without need.
senses.example: He worried needlessly about his dog.

core.definition: Without good reason or need; in a way that causes unnecessary trouble, harm, cost, or effort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NEE. The middle -less syllable is reduced to a short schwa, and the final -ly is pronounced lee, not lie.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies that the trouble or cost was avoidable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use needlessly to criticize something that caused trouble that did not have to happen, as in 'you needlessly worried me.' It is common in everyday speech and in writing. It often pairs with words like worry, complicate, spend, or risk. For a more neutral tone, use unnecessarily.

distinctions.note: Unnecessarily is more neutral and can describe anything excessive, while needlessly carries a judgment that the harm was avoidable.
Pointlessly stresses that the action has no purpose, while needlessly stresses that the trouble it caused was avoidable.

examples.everyday: Don't worry needlessly about the flight; they always get us there on time.
examples.professional: We needlessly duplicated the data pipeline, which doubled our cloud costs for three months.
examples.analytical: The argument needlessly multiplies entities, violating the principle of parsimony without gaining any explanatory power.

nuance.analogy: Like carrying an umbrella on a sunny day: the burden is real and the reason for it is absent.
nuance.etymology: From needless plus -ly; needless comes from need plus -less.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it NEED-less-lee with a long vowel in the middle; the middle syllable is weak (NEE-dluhs-lee).
Using needless as an adverb; needless is an adjective and needlessly is the adverb.

senses.definition: A pseudoscientific movement which attempts to reframe Christian creationism in more scientific terms, rather than citing Biblical scripture to support their claims.
senses.example: The school board debated whether neo-creationism belonged in the biology curriculum alongside evolution.

core.definition: A movement that presents Christian creationism in the language of science, such as claims about design in nature, instead of openly relying on Bible passages.

pronunciation.tip: Say 'neo' as NEE-oh, not 'nay-oh'. The main stress falls on the '-ay-' syllable of 'creationism', and the final syllable is weak. The word 'creation' is stressed in the middle, not at the start.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most usage. Critics use it to describe a movement they see as religious ideas dressed in scientific language, while its supporters usually reject the label.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'neo-creationism' mainly in academic writing, journalism, court cases and debates over school curricula. Supporters often prefer terms such as 'intelligent design' or 'creation science', so the word is usually used by critics. In casual talk, people more often say 'creationism' or 'intelligent design'.

distinctions.note: Intelligent design is one specific neo-creationist argument that some features of living things reflect intelligent causes; neo-creationism is the broader umbrella term.
Creationism is the general belief that God created the world, while neo-creationism refers specifically to newer efforts to frame that belief scientifically.

examples.everyday: My brother-in-law says the school board is pushing neo-creationism, but I'm not sure what they actually proposed.
examples.professional: Our science education policy memo should explicitly exclude neo-creationist material from the curriculum standards.
examples.analytical: Neo-creationism borrows the vocabulary of empirical inquiry while holding a theological conclusion fixed in advance.

nuance.analogy: Neo-creationism is like a sermon in a lab coat: the form looks scientific, but the conclusion was settled before the experiment began.
nuance.etymology: From Greek neos (new) combined with creationism, from Latin creatio (creation).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'neo-CREA-tion-ism', instead of the '-AY-' syllable.
Confusing neo-creationism with theistic evolution, which accepts evolution while affirming God as creator.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew verb bara' (בָּרָא, 'to create') is used in Genesis 1:1, where the RSV says that in the beginning God created the heavens and the earth. Genesis 1:27 says that God created humankind in his own image. Romans 1:20 says that God's invisible qualities have been clearly perceived through the things he has made, a verse often cited in arguments about design in nature.

traditions.view: Orthodox theology reads Genesis as a theological account of God as creator, drawing on Church Fathers such as Basil the Great, who interpreted the days in varied ways. There is no single Orthodox position on evolution or on the scientific reading of Genesis.

The Church affirms God as creator and holds that Scripture teaches this truth, while since Pius XII's 1950 encyclical Humani generis, Catholics have been allowed to study evolution scientifically. The Church holds that God directly creates each human soul.

Protestants hold a range of views: young-earth creationists, many of whom are Baptists or Pentecostals, reject common descent, while old-earth creationists and theistic evolutionists, often in Reformed, Lutheran or Anglican circles, accept an ancient earth and biological evolution under God's creative direction.

core.definition: An ancient city, capital of Assyria on the Tigris River, to which God sent the prophet Jonah to call for repentance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, NIN. The last two syllables are reduced to a soft 'vuh', not 'vay'. Do not stress the middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in ordinary speech. In Christian contexts it can carry the sense of a city that turned from wickedness to God.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the name mainly in Bible study, church, history, and archaeology. In casual talk it may refer to a 'Nineveh' as a symbol of a wicked city that repents. Pronounce it with the stress on the first syllable, as in the Bible readings many Americans hear.

distinctions.note: Assyria was the empire or region; Nineveh was its capital city.
Babylon was the great city of Babylonian power; Nineveh was the Assyrian capital, and in the Bible it is linked with a city that God judges and then spares.

examples.everyday: Have you heard the story about Jonah and the whale and the city of Nineveh?
examples.professional: Our archaeology team's report describes the ruins of Nineveh near modern Mosul.
examples.analytical: The Book of Nahum pronounces judgment on Nineveh, while Jonah shows God's willingness to spare the same city when it repents.

nuance.analogy: Like a famous city whose name stands for a whole story: say 'Nineveh' and a Bible reader thinks of the city that turned from its evil ways.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ninewe (נִינְוֵה), a name of the Assyrian city.
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable, as in nin-IH-vuh.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'vay' instead of a reduced 'vuh'.
nuance.biblical_note: Nineveh (Hebrew Ninewe) was the great capital of Assyria, the empire that threatened Israel for centuries. In Scripture it stands for imperial power and cruelty, yet God's call to it shows his concern for Gentile nations as well. Genesis 10:11 says Asshur built Nineveh. Jonah 1:2 has God send Jonah to Nineveh to cry against its wickedness. Jonah 3:5-10 describes the Ninevites believing, fasting, and turning from evil, so God relents from the judgment. Nahum 3:1-7 pronounces doom on the 'bloody city' of Nineveh, which fell in 612 BC.

senses.definition: Of or relating to nomads.
Of or related to itinerant herdsmen.
senses.example: The nomadic families moved their goats and sheep across the steppe with each season.

senses.definition: Of or related to any habitually wandering person or animal.
senses.example: After college, Jake lived a nomadic life, sleeping in hostels and never staying in one city for long.

core.definition: Relating to a lifestyle of moving from place to place without a permanent home.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the middle syllable, MAD, not on the first. The final ic is short and light, so say 'MAD-ik' with a quick ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a way of life; can be positive when romantic, negative when it implies a lack of stability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nomadic for peoples, animals, and lifestyles, such as a nomadic tribe or nomadic work. It is common in travel writing, anthropology, and business talk about remote work. Use it as an adjective only; for the person, say nomad.

distinctions.note: Itinerant is more formal and suggests traveling for work, such as a preacher or judge on circuit.
Migratory usually refers to animals or seasonal movement between fixed areas; nomadic implies no fixed home.
Mobile describes being able to move; nomadic describes a way of life based on moving.

examples.everyday: My cousin has a nomadic lifestyle, so she is hard to pin down for dinner.
examples.professional: Our product supports a nomadic workflow, so engineers can start a task on a laptop and finish it on a phone.
examples.analytical: Heidegger's critique of modern dwelling suggests that a nomadic existence can conceal a deeper failure to belong anywhere.

nuance.analogy: Nomadic life is like a river that keeps moving to find new ground rather than settling into a single lake.
nuance.etymology: From nomad plus the suffix -ic, from Greek nomadikos, 'of wandering herders'.
common_mistakes: Using nomadic as a noun, as in 'a nomadic' for a person; say nomad.
Stressing the first syllable, as in NOH-mad-ik.

senses.definition: A person named, or designated, by another, to any office, duty, or position; one nominated, or proposed, by others for office or for election to office.
senses.example: The committee announced its nominee for the vacant council seat on Monday.

senses.definition: A person or organization in whose name a security is registered though true ownership is held by another party, called nominator, especially for the purpose of concealing the identity of the nominator.
senses.example: The Supreme Court confiscated half of Thaksin Shinawatra's fortune after finding that, while being Prime Minister, he held shares in commercial companies through nominees.

senses.definition: A person to whom the holder of a copyhold estate surrenders their interest.
senses.example: The steward recorded that the copyhold had passed to the nominee after the surrender.

core.definition: A person who has been formally proposed for a job, prize, or election and is being considered.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the final syllable, which sounds like 'knee'. Many learners say 'NOM-ih-ny' with the wrong stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it simply means someone is being considered.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nominee for people proposed for government posts, board seats, or awards, such as 'the Supreme Court nominee'. It is not used for a casual group choice like picking a restaurant. The verb form is 'nominate'.

distinctions.note: A nominee has been formally nominated by someone; a candidate may simply be running for office.
A nominee has not yet been confirmed; an appointee already holds the position.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor is the nominee for the school board, so there are yard signs everywhere.
examples.professional: The committee will interview the nominee for the director role next Tuesday.
examples.analytical: A nominee holds a provisional status: named by another, but not yet vested with the office.

nuance.analogy: A nominee is like a name on a draft list: chosen to be considered, but not yet on the roster.
nuance.etymology: From French nommé 'named', from Latin nominare 'to name'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'NOM-ih-nee'.
Using nominee for a casual choice rather than a formal selection process.

conversation.text: She's a nominee for best supporting actress.
All the nominees looked nervous before they announced the winner.
The nominees are announced in January.

senses.definition: Not associative.
Whose multiplication operation is not assumed to be associative for all elements.
senses.example: Octonion multiplication is nonassociative, so the grouping of factors can change the product.

core.definition: Not associative: an operation where changing the grouping of operands can change the result, so (a·b)·c may differ from a·(b·c).

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SO in associative, and shee is one syllable, not two. The final -tive ends with a short i, so say tiv, not tive.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is an exact mathematical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in abstract algebra, computer science, and advanced math courses, usually to describe an operation or algebra. It is rare in everyday speech. Do not confuse it with noncommutative, which is about order rather than grouping. A teacher might say, 'Subtraction is nonassociative, so the parentheses matter.'

distinctions.note: Noncommutative means a times b can differ from b times a; nonassociative means changing the grouping can change the result, so the two are separate properties.
Associative means grouping never changes the result, while nonassociative means at least one grouping can change it, so it is the negation of the property.

examples.professional: The team's proof assumes that the multiplication is nonassociative, so we cannot rearrange the parentheses the way we usually do.
examples.analytical: Octonion multiplication is nonassociative, which changes how we interpret symmetry and rotation in higher dimensions.

nuance.analogy: Nonassociative operations are like stacking blocks in different orders: the way you group the first two changes the final tower.
nuance.etymology: From non- and associative, from associate, from Latin associare 'to join with'.
common_mistakes: Confusing nonassociative with noncommutative; nonassociative is about grouping, not order.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying ah-so-SHEE-ah-tive instead of uh-SOH-shee-uh-tiv.

senses.definition: Not combustible.
senses.example: Our lab coats are made from nonflammable fabric, which is required near the solvent cabinets.

senses.definition: Not easily set on fire.
Any nonflammable substance.
senses.example: Keep every solvent bottle away from heat, since many nonflammables still release toxic vapors.

core.definition: Unable to catch fire or burn easily; not flammable, so it is safe to use or store near heat or flame.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NON, and the 'a' in 'flam' is the short vowel of 'flam' rather than 'flame.' The ending '-able' reduces to 'uh-bul.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, since it describes safety. It is commonly seen on labels and in safety rules.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see this word on product labels, building codes and safety signs, so it is very common in practical life. The noun use, as in 'any nonflammable substance,' is less common than the adjective. People often say 'flame-retardant' when they mean a material treated to resist fire.

distinctions.note: Fireproof suggests a thing cannot be damaged by fire, while nonflammable only means it will not catch fire easily.
Flame-retardant describes a material treated to slow burning, while nonflammable describes a material that does not burn at all.

examples.everyday: Get the nonflammable kind of cleaner for the garage, since we keep the paint and the water heater in there.
examples.professional: The new insulation is nonflammable and meets the fire code for commercial buildings.
examples.analytical: Calling a material nonflammable is a claim about a specific test condition, not an absolute property of the substance.

nuance.analogy: A wet log in the fireplace can be lit, but it refuses to sustain the blaze, which is what nonflammable means.
nuance.etymology: Non- plus flammable, from Latin flamma 'flame'.
common_mistakes: Assuming inflammable means not burnable; in English it means flammable, which is why the word nonflammable is preferred.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'non-FLAM-uh-bul'; the main stress is on NON.

senses.definition: The fact of not participating in some activity or event.
senses.example: Voluntary nonparticipation in the work force is a growing problem in some developed countries.

core.definition: The fact of not taking part in an activity, event, or process.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on PAY, the -ation syllable. The ending is 'ay-shun' with a clear sh sound, not 'see-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in research and civic settings, but often negative when it suggests apathy, as in low voter nonparticipation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in politics, research, and workplace reports, as in 'low voter nonparticipation' or 'nonparticipation rates'. In conversation, people usually say 'not voting' or 'not taking part'. Using nonparticipation in casual talk sounds formal and a bit detached.

distinctions.note: Abstention means deliberately refusing to vote or decide, while nonparticipation is broader and need not be deliberate.
Absenteeism is regular, often unexcused absence from work or school; nonparticipation can mean not joining an activity, not just being absent.

examples.everyday: Her nonparticipation in the office pool made me think she just didn't want to join in.
examples.professional: The report shows a 20 percent nonparticipation rate among employees who were invited to the training.
examples.analytical: Political theorists debate whether nonparticipation in elections reflects consent, apathy, or a principled refusal to take part.

nuance.analogy: It's like a passenger who never boards the bus: the trip goes on without them.
nuance.etymology: non- (Latin 'not') plus participation, from Latin participatio 'sharing', from participare.
common_mistakes: Using nonparticipation in casual conversation where 'not taking part' sounds more natural.
Placing the stress on the wrong syllable; it falls on PAY, not on the prefix or on tis.

senses.definition: In a nostalgic manner.

core.definition: In a way that fondly remembers or longs for the past, often with a bittersweet feeling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'STAL' in the middle of the word. The vowel is the short, open sound of 'cot,' not 'aw,' and the final -ly sounds like 'lee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or bittersweet; warm, with some sadness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb when describing memories, songs, or old places, such as 'She talked nostalgically about her college dorm.' It is a little literary for casual speech, so in conversation people often say 'I miss those days' instead. It fits writing, toasts, and reflective talk.

distinctions.note: Wistfully implies a sad longing, often for something out of reach; nostalgically implies fond memories, usually with less regret.
Sentimentally focuses on emotional attachment, which can be overdone; nostalgically is about looking back with warm feeling at a time.

examples.everyday: We drove past our old high school, and she smiled nostalgically.
examples.professional: In the retirement speech, the director spoke nostalgically about the early days of the team, then outlined next year's goals.
examples.analytical: The novel describes its childhood setting nostalgically, but the narrator's descriptions reveal the idealization that memory performs.

nuance.analogy: Like flipping through an old photo album and smiling at pictures of a place you can no longer visit.
nuance.etymology: From 'nostalgia,' coined in 1688 from Greek nostos 'return home' and algos 'pain.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the middle one, 'STAL'.
Treating 'nostalgia' as a countable noun; it is usually uncountable.

senses.definition: A short novel, synonymous with novella.
A story longer than a short story, but shorter than a novella.
A short piece of lyrical music, especially one for the piano.
senses.example: The pianist played a delicate novelette by Schumann, full of lyrical melodies.

core.definition: A work of fiction longer than a short story but shorter than a novella, usually about 7,500 to 17,500 words.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the last syllable, LET, which rhymes with 'bet'. The first two syllables are quick and reduced, so do not stress the 'nov' part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise category term rather than an emotional word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'novelette' mainly in publishing, writing workshops, and literary awards, such as the Hugo and Nebula categories for science fiction. In everyday speech, people usually say 'a short story' or 'a novella'. Using it for a full novel will confuse American writers.

distinctions.note: A novella is longer than a novelette, usually about 17,500 to 40,000 words, and is more common in American publishing for short book-length fiction.
A short story is usually much shorter, often under 7,500 words, while a novelette is a longer piece with more room for character and plot.

examples.everyday: I read a novelette on the train, so I finished it before my stop.
examples.professional: The anthology accepted my submission as a novelette, so the editors placed it between the short stories and the novellas.
examples.analytical: The novelette's compressed form forces the author to develop character and conflict faster than a full novel allows.

nuance.analogy: Like a short film: it has a complete story, but it is not the full-length feature.
nuance.etymology: From novel plus the French diminutive suffix -ette, 'little'.
common_mistakes: Using 'novelette' for a full-length novel; Americans would call that a 'novel'.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'NOV-uh-let', instead of the final syllable.

senses.definition: Having nuances; possessed of multiple layers of detail, pattern, or meaning.
senses.example: The setting sunlight played through the gently waving branches, creating subtly nuanced transitions of color and tone.

core.definition: Showing subtle differences, layers of detail, or shades of meaning rather than a simple, one-sided view.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ed is silent after the n, so the word ends in a single 't' sound, like 'nst'. Learners often add an extra 'ed' syllable, which is incorrect.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises analysis, writing, or a viewpoint that is careful and fair rather than simplistic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nuanced to praise a thoughtful argument, a balanced article, or a careful view of a complex issue. It is common in reviews, school writing, news commentary, and workplace discussions. In casual talk, people might say 'it's complicated' instead, but 'nuanced' is a respected word to use in professional settings.

distinctions.note: Complex describes something with many parts, while nuanced describes how carefully those parts are treated or shown.
Subtle describes something hard to notice, while nuanced describes a careful, layered treatment of a topic.

examples.everyday: Her take on the city's new parking plan was really nuanced, not just a yes or no.
examples.professional: We need a nuanced approach to the data, because the averages hide big differences between regions.
examples.analytical: A nuanced reading of the parable resists both literalism and allegory, attending to its tensions and its context.

nuance.analogy: A nuanced view is like a detailed map instead of a single arrow: it shows the roads, hills, and detours, not just the direction.
nuance.etymology: Derived from nuance, from French nuance, 'shade of color.'
common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable at the end, pronouncing it 'NOO-ahn-sed'.
Using nuanced to mean 'complicated' in every case; it specifically praises careful, layered thinking.

senses.definition: Without clothing or other covering of the skin; without clothing on the genitals or female nipples.
senses.example: Why do you act so prudish whenever you see nude people?

senses.definition: Of a color (such as beige or tan) that evokes bare flesh.
A painting, sculpture, photograph or other artwork or mass-media-reproduced image depicting one or more human figure(s) in a state of near or total undress.
senses.example: Michelangelo's David is a well-known standing male nude; Michelangelo also created several other nudes.

senses.definition: The state of total nudity.
senses.example: she caught him in the nude

senses.definition: A color that resembles or evokes bare flesh; a paint, dye, etc. of such color.

core.definition: Without any clothes on; naked. In art and fashion it can also describe a flesh-toned color.

pronunciation.tip: Use the long oo of 'food' with a clear, final d. Do not add a y sound (not 'nyood') in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in art, medicine and fashion; can sound sexual or provocative in casual conversation, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'naked' in ordinary talk ('he was running around naked'); 'nude' sounds more formal, artistic or clinical, as in 'nude model' or 'nude painting'. In fashion, 'nude' means a skin-toned shade, as in 'nude heels'. The term 'nude beach' is common, but saying someone was 'nude' in casual conversation may sound unexpectedly stiff or suggestive.

distinctions.note: Naked is the everyday, plain word for having no clothes on; nude is more formal or artistic and can sound clinical or suggestive.
Undressed describes the act or state of taking clothes off, often temporarily; nude describes the state of being without clothes in a fixed, descriptive way.
Bare means uncovered or exposed, as in bare feet or a bare wall; nude refers specifically to a person or figure without clothes.

examples.everyday: The toddler ran nude from the bath to the hallway, giggling the whole way.
examples.professional: The art department needs a nude model for the life drawing class next Tuesday, so please confirm your availability.
examples.analytical: Renaissance painters often used the nude body to explore ideal human proportion, which made the human form a moral and philosophical subject.

nuance.analogy: Nude is like a formal portrait of naked: the same bare state, seen through the frame of art or form.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nudus, meaning naked or bare.
common_mistakes: Using nude as a casual synonym for naked in everyday conversation, where it can sound stiff or sexual.
Pronouncing it with a y sound, as 'nyood'.

nude.etymology: Entered English 1493 as a legal term, meaning "unsupported, not formally attested," from Middle English *nud*, from Latin *nūdus* (“naked, bare”).

senses.definition: Someone who is insane.
senses.example: Our neighbor is a total nutcase who talks to his lawn mower.

core.definition: An informal word for an odd, eccentric person, or sometimes someone who seems mentally unstable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, 'nut,' with a short 'uh' vowel. The second word, 'case,' has secondary stress and rhymes with 'face,' so don't reduce it to 'kiss.'

nuance.connotation: Negative or playful, depending on tone. It can be affectionate between friends but insulting when said about a stranger.
nuance.usage_note: 'Nutcase' is slang, so use it with friends or family in relaxed talk, not at work or with people you don't know well. Americans often say it playfully, as in 'Oh, he's a total nutcase, but I love him.' A natural reply is a laugh and a comment like 'Yeah, he's definitely one of a kind.' To be more polite, say 'eccentric' or 'a character.'

distinctions.note: 'Eccentric' is polite and describes unusual behavior, while 'nutcase' is informal and can be insulting.
Both are informal and slightly rude, but 'weirdo' focuses on strange behavior, while 'nutcase' can suggest mental instability.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a bit of a nutcase, but he always shovels our driveway after snowstorms.
examples.professional: Don't let the nutcase in the code review thread distract you; focus on the test failures.
examples.analytical: Calling a political opponent a nutcase substitutes a personal insult for a substantive argument about policy.

nuance.analogy: A nutcase is like a clock that runs on its own rhythm, out of step with everyone else around it.
nuance.etymology: Slang compound of nut, a slang word for the head or mind, and case.
common_mistakes: Using 'nutcase' about someone with a serious mental illness; this is hurtful and can be offensive.
Writing it as 'nut case' in some contexts; both spellings are accepted, but 'nutcase' is more common.

senses.definition: The testicles.
senses.example: He took a hard hit to the nuts during the game and had to sit down.

senses.definition: An unbeatable hand; the best poker hand available.
senses.example: If the board is 237QA, all of spades, the nuts is 45 of spades.

senses.definition: Insane, mad.
senses.example: After living on the island alone for five years, he eventually went nuts.

senses.definition: Crazy, mad; unusually pleased or, alternatively, angered.
senses.example: I just go nuts over her fantastic desserts.

senses.definition: Very fond of (on) someone.
senses.example: He's been nuts on her since the day they met.

senses.definition: Indicates annoyance, anger, or disappointment.
senses.example: Nuts! They didn't even listen to what I had to say.

senses.definition: Signifies rejection of a proposal or idea, as in forget it, no way, or nothing doing; often followed by to, as nuts to.
senses.example: They want me to pay $5 for a banana? Nuts to that!

core.definition: Informal: crazy or insane, or extremely excited or enthusiastic about someone or something.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'uh' vowel and end with a crisp 'ts' sound. Do not add a vowel between the t and s, and avoid the 'oo' sound of 'nut' in some other languages.

nuance.connotation: Informal and mild in most uses, but the word can be rude. The testicles sense is vulgar, and 'nuts' can sound harsh when used about people with mental health conditions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'nuts' mainly in casual speech: 'go nuts' means become very excited or angry, 'drive someone nuts' means annoy them, and 'nuts about' means love. Calling someone 'nuts' is a casual insult, so use it carefully with people you do not know well. The slang sense for testicles is vulgar and should be avoided in polite company.

distinctions.note: Crazy is the most general word and can be used seriously. Nuts is more playful and casual, and often describes something that is annoying or extreme.
Bonkers is mainly British and sounds more playful. Nuts is the American word for a similar idea.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's dog goes nuts every time the fireworks start.
examples.professional: The release schedule is nuts, but if we cut the scope we can still ship by Friday.
examples.analytical: Dismissing the proposal as nuts spares the author from answering its premises, which is a poor substitute for argument.

nuance.analogy: Nuts is like a pressure valve on a kettle: when the feeling builds up, it lets out a loud, quick expression of how wild the situation feels.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hnutu, 'nut.' The slang sense of 'crazy' is a later figurative extension from 'nut' used for the head, in 20th-century American slang.
common_mistakes: Using 'nuts' in formal writing or serious medical contexts, where it sounds rude. Use 'insane' or 'unstable' instead.
Assuming 'nuts' only means crazy. In American speech, 'nuts about someone' means you love them.

senses.definition: Of or relating to an obituary.
senses.example: an obituarial notice in the newspaper

core.definition: Relating to an obituary, or having the factual, summarizing tone of an obituary.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AIR, the -er- syllable, with the -ial ending reduced to 'ee-uhl.' Many learners pronounce the middle as 'bit-chew,' which is correct, but they add an extra w sound that is not standard.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a tone or structure rather than praising or criticizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use obituarial. They more often say 'like an obituary' or 'obituary-style' in everyday speech. In writing, the word appears in literary criticism and reviews to describe a summarizing or retrospective tone. Use it when you want to describe a text that reads like a summary of a life or a career.

distinctions.note: Elegiac describes mourning or lament, often in poetry. Obituarial describes a factual, summarizing tone.
Necrological relates to lists or records of the dead. Obituarial focuses on the summary of a life.

examples.everyday: His toast had an obituarial tone, listing everything Grandpa had done, which made the party feel more like a funeral.
examples.professional: The project memo had an obituarial feel, recounting our achievements as if the project were already closed.
examples.analytical: Her biography adopts an obituarial structure, moving from birth and marriage to a tidy summary of achievements, and so leaves the subject's doubts out.

nuance.analogy: Like a tombstone that reads like a résumé: accurate, brief and final.
nuance.etymology: From obituary, from Medieval Latin obituarium, plus the suffix -al (relating to).
common_mistakes: Using obituarial in casual conversation, where obituary-style is more natural.
Pronouncing the middle as bit-chew-ary with the stress in the wrong place. The stress belongs on the -er- syllable.

senses.definition: To rebuke or scold strongly.
To remonstrate, complain, to rail against.
senses.example: Rather than objurgate the staff, the manager calmly asked everyone to explain what had gone wrong.

core.definition: To scold or rebuke someone harshly, often at length.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak er sound, and the g is hard as in get, followed by a long ay.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes a harsh, sustained scolding.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare word in American speech and mostly appears in literature or formal writing. Americans would more often say scold, chew out, or tear into someone. Using it in casual conversation can sound pretentious.

distinctions.note: Scold is everyday and suggests reprimanding someone for a small fault, while objurgate is formal and suggests a longer, harsher rebuke.
Reprimand is a formal, often official rebuke in a workplace, while objurgate is more literary and emphatic.
Berate means to criticize angrily and at length, and it is more common in American English than objurgate.

examples.professional: The director objurgated the team for missing the deadline, which left everyone demoralized.
examples.analytical: The prophet objurgates a people who have forgotten their covenant, and the force of the rebuke is the point.

nuance.analogy: It is like a parent's long, stern lecture rather than a quick reminder.
nuance.etymology: From Latin objurgare, to chide, from ob- plus jurgare, to quarrel.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable or pronouncing the g as a j sound.
Using it as a noun; the noun is objurgation.

senses.definition: A type of naturally occurring black glass produced by volcanoes.
A slightly bluish black, the color of obsidian glass.
senses.example: obsidian:

senses.definition: (poetic) Black.
senses.label: poetic

core.definition: A dark, glassy volcanic rock that forms when lava cools quickly, with a smooth surface that breaks into sharp edges.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SID. The last syllable is a soft 'un', not a full 'ian'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, a descriptive term for a natural material or a dark color.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'obsidian' in geology, archaeology, jewelry, and fantasy writing, and as a color name for a deep, glossy black. It is not an everyday word for most people, but you may hear it in museum talk or in product descriptions. Outside those settings, people usually say 'black glass' or 'volcanic glass.'

distinctions.note: Basalt is a dark volcanic rock that is crystalline and dull, while obsidian is glassy and smooth because it cooled too fast for crystals to form.
Jet is a black organic fossil material, whereas obsidian is a black volcanic glass.

examples.everyday: That little polished stone on the shelf is obsidian, from a volcano in Oregon.
examples.professional: The museum's catalog lists the arrowhead as obsidian, sourced from a quarry in Idaho.
examples.analytical: Obsidian's conchoidal fracture made it prized by early toolmakers, who could shape razor-sharp edges from it.

nuance.analogy: Obsidian is like frozen lava that cooled so quickly it never had time to form crystals, leaving a smooth, shiny glass.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obsidianus, a word attributed to the Roman naturalist Pliny, possibly from the name of a Roman discoverer, Obsius.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as 'ob-SIH-dee-an' with an emphasis on the final syllable.
Confusing obsidian with 'opal' or 'onyx' because all are stones.

obsidian.etymology: From Latin *obsidianus*; named after *Obsidius*, who was, according to Pliny, the Roman who discovered the stone in Aethiopia.

senses.definition: To become or be rendered obsolete; to undergo obsolescence.
senses.example: ; see also Thesaurus:to age

core.definition: To become obsolete, or go out of use or date as newer products, technologies or ideas take their place.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on LES, which rhymes with less, and the first syllable has light secondary stress. Do not add an extra syllable at the end, and do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a natural process; in business it can sound slightly negative for the thing becoming outdated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans more often say become obsolete or go obsolete in conversation. Obsolesce is mainly found in technical writing, business analysis and economics. You will hear the noun obsolescence far more often, as in planned obsolescence. A simpler phrase often sounds more natural in a meeting.

distinctions.note: Become obsolete is the everyday American phrase and is more common in conversation, while obsolesce is shorter and more technical.
Expire suggests reaching an end date, such as a contract or coupon, while obsolesce describes falling out of use because something better exists.
Age describes gradual change over time, while obsolesce specifically means losing value or use because of newer alternatives.

examples.everyday: I think my old flip phone is starting to obsolesce, since nobody can text on it anymore.
examples.professional: We should design these APIs so older versions can obsolesce gradually over two releases.
examples.analytical: Schumpeter's account of creative destruction explains why productive capital may obsolesce long before it physically wears out.

nuance.analogy: Like a paper map after the GPS app arrives, it still exists but no longer serves its purpose.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obsolescere, to fall into disuse, from obsoletus, worn out or disused.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as OB-suh-less instead of putting the main stress on LES.
Confusing the verb obsolesce with the adjective obsolete.

obsolesce.etymology: From Latin *obsolescere* (“to wear out, fall into disuse, grow old, decay”), from *ob-* + *olesco* (“to grow”).

senses.definition: The characteristic of being obstinate.
senses.example: His obstinance in refusing every compromise kept the negotiations stalled for months.

core.definition: Stubborn refusal to change one's opinion or course of action, even when good reasons are offered.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, OB, so say AHB-stih-nuns. The middle -stin- is short, and the final -ance is a weak, reduced vowel. Learners often stress the second syllable or give the last syllable a long a.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying stubbornness that ignores evidence or reason.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use obstinance; they usually say obstinacy, stubbornness or simply stubborn. You will mostly meet the word in older books or formal essays. In conversation, say he's being stubborn, and reserve obstinance for writing where you want a formal tone.
