senses.example: The archer took a sitting shot at the deer from the blind.

senses.definition: Occupying a specific official or legal position; incumbent.
senses.example: The sitting governor is expected to win reelection easily this November.

senses.definition: Of a bird, incubating eggs.
senses.example: The sitting hen refused to leave the nest, even when we approached.

core.definition: A period when a group is seated and served, or a session when someone sits for a portrait or photo.

pronunciation.tip: The first syllable is stressed and the ending is a short 'ing', not 'eeng'. In fast speech the tt becomes a flap, so it sounds like 'SID-ing'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a routine event with no special feeling attached.
nuance.usage_note: In restaurants, hosts often announce 'We have two sittings for dinner,' meaning the early or late group of guests. A sitting for a portrait or photo is a session, and 'in one sitting' means finished in a single go. The adjective sense, meaning current holder of an office, appears mostly in news or legal writing.

distinctions.note: A sitting is a session or serving period; seating is the arrangement of seats or the number of seats available.
Session is broader and can mean any meeting or period of activity; sitting usually refers to a specific time when people are seated.

examples.everyday: The host said our table is ready for the second sitting, so we can eat at eight thirty.
examples.professional: Each training sitting is limited to twenty people, so please register by Friday.
examples.analytical: A single sitting with the text let her read the whole argument without interruption, which changed how she judged its structure.

nuance.analogy: A sitting is like a train departure: a fixed time when a group boards together.
nuance.etymology: From the verb sit plus the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Using sitting for the seat itself; a seat or chair is the usual word.
Confusing 'in one sitting' with 'in one seat', which is a different meaning.

senses.definition: Hot enough to make a hissing sound.
Brought to the table in the metal dish it has been cooked in, making such a sound.
senses.example: The waiter set a sizzling skillet of fajitas on our table and the peppers hissed loudly.

senses.definition: Exciting and intensely emotional or sexual.
Very skillful or impressive.
senses.example: The two teams played a sizzling match.

senses.definition: Such a hissing sound.
senses.example: Over the sizzling of the grill, I could barely hear the phone ringing in the kitchen.

core.definition: Very hot and making a hissing sound while cooking; also used for something intensely exciting or sexually charged.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. Keep the z voiced and the le as a syllabic l. End with a short 'ing', not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Positive for food and weather; in romance or marketing, it is positive but can be sensual, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sizzling for steak, fajitas, or a skillet just out of the oven, and 'sizzling hot' for weather. Restaurants often bring sizzling plates on hot iron platters. Figurative uses such as 'sizzling chemistry' or 'a sizzling new album' are common in media and sound upbeat.

distinctions.note: Scorching means extremely hot in a damaging way, as in a scorching summer; sizzling suggests food or surfaces that are hot and making a hissing sound.
Hot is a neutral, general word; sizzling is vivid and suggests active heat, often with sound.

examples.everyday: The fajitas came out on a sizzling platter, and the whole table cheered.
examples.professional: Our sizzling growth in the Midwest is great, but support staffing has not kept pace.
examples.analytical: The sizzling market rally of that year masked weakness in underlying earnings.

nuance.analogy: Like bacon just out of the pan: the heat is visible and audible at the same time.
nuance.etymology: From sizzle plus the -ing suffix used to form adjectives.
common_mistakes: Using sizzling for food that is hot but silent
Pronouncing the z as an s
Using sizzling as a verb instead of sizzle, as in 'I sizzling the steak'

senses.definition: To make a brief, basic drawing.
senses.example: I usually sketch with a pen rather than a pencil.

senses.definition: To describe briefly and with very few details.
senses.example: He sketched the accident, sticking to the facts as they had happened.

senses.definition: A rapidly executed freehand drawing that is not intended as a finished work, often consisting of a multitude of overlapping lines.
A rough design, plan, or draft, as a rough draft of a book.
senses.example: The architect showed the client a rough sketch of the proposed library before drafting plans.

senses.definition: A brief description of a person or account of an incident; a general presentation or outline.
senses.example: I have to write a character sketch for a novel study.

senses.definition: A brief, light, or unfinished dramatic, musical, or literary work or idea; especially a short, often humorous or satirical scene or play, frequently as part of a revue or variety show.
senses.example: The comedy troupe performed a sharp political sketch during the late-night variety show.

senses.definition: A brief musical composition or theme, especially for the piano.
senses.example: She played a short sketch by Grieg as an encore after the recital.

senses.definition: A brief, light, or informal literary composition, such as an essay or short story.
senses.example: The magazine published her brief sketch about growing up in a small Ohio town.

senses.definition: An amusing person.
senses.example: Everyone adored Uncle Mike; he was such a sketch at family dinners.

senses.definition: A formal specification of a mathematical structure or a data type described in terms of a graph and diagrams (and cones (and cocones)) on it. It can be implemented by means of “models”, which are functors which are graph homomorphisms from the formal specification to categories such that the diagrams become commutative, the cones become limiting (i.e. products), the cocones become colimiting (i.e. sums).
senses.example: In category theory, the data type is specified by a sketch whose diagrams must commute in each model.

senses.definition: Sketchy, shady, questionable.
senses.example: That used-car deal looked sketch, so I walked away from the lot.

senses.definition: Fascist or with right-wing or neo-Nazi ties; NSBM.
senses.example: Journalists documented the sketch ties of the party's youth wing to neo-Nazi groups.

core.definition: A quick, rough drawing made freehand, not meant as a finished work, often built from loose overlapping lines.

pronunciation.tip: This one-syllable word has a short e as in bed, and the tch is a single sound, so it rhymes with fetch. Do not add an extra t or stretch the vowel into ski.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; a sketch is casual and quick, but as a description it can suggest something unfinished or vague.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sketch for a quick drawing, a rough plan, a short description, or a comedy skit on TV, such as sketches on Saturday Night Live. For a finished drawing, say drawing or painting, since a sketch is expected to be rough. Be careful with the adjective sense, sketchy, which is informal slang for shady or questionable.

distinctions.note: A draft is a fuller working version of a text or plan, while a sketch is quicker and rougher.
An outline lists main points in order; a sketch can be a drawing or a loose description with few details.
A doodle is an idle scribble; a sketch is deliberate, though still quick.

examples.everyday: The artist at the park did a quick sketch of my dog in about five minutes.
examples.professional: Send me a rough sketch of the dashboard layout, and we can refine it in Thursday's meeting.
examples.analytical: Augustine's sketch of the two cities is broad, giving an outline of salvation history rather than its detailed course.

nuance.analogy: A sketch is like a map drawn on a napkin: enough to find your way, but not a full survey.
nuance.etymology: From Dutch schets, from Italian schizzo, ultimately from Greek skhedios, meaning done offhand.
common_mistakes: Using sketch for a finished piece; a sketch is expected to be rough.
Pronouncing the vowel as a long ee, as in ski, instead of the short e in SKECH.

sketch.etymology: From Dutch *schets* or German *Skizze*, from Italian *schizzo*, from Latin *schedium*, from Ancient Greek *σχέδιος* (“made suddenly, off-hand”), from *σχεδόν* (“near, nearby”), from *ἔχω* (“to hold”).

senses.definition: To creep out; to give a creepy or sketchy feeling to someone.
senses.example: The awkward and agitated customer began to sketch them out a bit.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see sketch,‎ out.
senses.example: I sketched out the trees and the lake before adding texture and color to the scene.

core.definition: To describe or draw the main outline of something roughly, without giving every detail.

pronunciation.tip: The stress usually falls on out in this phrasal verb, so say skech OWT. In fast speech the two words link smoothly with no pause.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing a plan; the slang sense, to make someone uneasy, is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say sketch out a plan or idea at work, meaning to give the main points before the details. In casual speech, sketch someone out means to make them uneasy, as in That guy really sketches me out. A natural reply to a request is Sure, let me sketch it out for you.

distinctions.note: Outline is a more formal word for listing main points; sketch out suggests a rougher, quicker version.
Map out means to plan in detail, while sketch out stays more general and provisional.

examples.everyday: Can you sketch out the route for us before we leave?
examples.professional: Let's sketch out the rollout timeline in the next meeting and fill in the details later.
examples.analytical: Rawls sketches out a theory of justice in broad strokes, leaving the institutional details for later.

nuance.analogy: Like tracing the rough shape of a house on paper before drawing the walls.
common_mistakes: Placing the object between sketch and out, as in sketch the plan out, which is correct but less natural than sketch out a plan.
Using sketch someone out to mean outline something; that phrase means to make someone uneasy.

senses.definition: The property of being sketchy.
senses.example: The sketchiness of the contractor's estimate made me hire someone else.

core.definition: The quality of being incomplete, vague, or of doubtful reliability or safety.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable; the ending -iness reduces to ih-nus, not ee-ness. The ch is one sound, and the t does not separate it.

nuance.connotation: Negative; the quality suggests doubt, risk or incomplete information.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sketchiness to describe a vague plan, a shady deal, or a neighborhood that feels unsafe. It is usually said with a judgment, as in the sketchiness of the data. It is a fairly mild word, but it suggests suspicion more than outright proof of wrongdoing.

distinctions.note: Vagueness is a lack of clear meaning; sketchiness adds a sense of incomplete or unreliable information.
Shadiness suggests dishonesty; sketchiness can simply mean incomplete or uncertain.

examples.everyday: I didn't like the sketchiness of that parking lot late at night.
examples.professional: Management noticed the sketchiness of the project timeline and asked for more detail.
examples.analytical: The sketchiness of the early manuscript makes it hard to date and harder to interpret reliably.

nuance.analogy: Like a photo taken in fog: the shapes are there, but the edges are missing.
common_mistakes: Using sketchiness for a finished drawing; it describes incompleteness or doubtful quality.
Stressing the second syllable, as in skuh-CHEE-nus.

senses.definition: A small flat-bottomed open boat with a pointed bow and square stern.
Any of various types of boats small enough for sailing or rowing by one person.
senses.example: We rented a small skiff and rowed across the bay before sunrise.

senses.definition: A light, fleeting shower of rain or snow, or gust of wind, etc.
senses.example: A skiff of rain blew into the shed and the two men moved their chairs back.

senses.definition: A (typically light) dusting of snow or ice (or dust, etc) (on ground, water, trees, etc).
senses.example: A light skiff of snow covered the lawn when we woke up.

senses.definition: An act of slightly pruning tea bushes, placing new leaves at a convenient height without removing much woody growth.
senses.example: The skiff this spring left the bushes at a convenient height for plucking.

senses.definition: To cut (a tea bush) to maintain the plucking table.
senses.example: Workers skiff the tea bushes every spring to keep the plucking table level.

senses.definition: To navigate in a skiff.
senses.example: We skiffed across the lagoon at dawn, rowing quietly past the sleeping herons.

core.definition: A small, light, flat-bottomed open boat, usually rowed or sailed by one or two people.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short i of kit and end with a clear f, not a v. Do not add a vowel between the sk and the i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, sometimes romantic in literature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use skiff mainly in literature, fishing, and coastal or Gulf Coast contexts, and in boating terms. In everyday talk, people say rowboat, dinghy, or small boat. Skiff is recognized but not common in casual speech.

distinctions.note: A dinghy is a small boat often carried or used as a tender for a larger yacht; a skiff is a flat-bottomed open boat rowed or sailed on its own.
A canoe is pointed at both ends and usually paddled, while a skiff has a square stern and may be rowed or motored.

examples.everyday: We rented a skiff at the lake and spent the whole afternoon fishing near the dock.
examples.professional: The marina's rental fleet includes three aluminum skiffs for guest use, with life jackets stored in each one.
examples.analytical: In the sea novel, the small skiff becomes a symbol of human fragility against the vast and indifferent ocean.

nuance.analogy: Like a bathtub with a pointed front, carried across open water.
nuance.etymology: From French esquif, probably from Italian schifo, from a Germanic root meaning ship.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing skiff with a long ee sound, as in skeef.
Using skiff for a yacht or large sailboat, which are much bigger.

skiff.etymology: From Middle English *skif*, from Middle French *esquif*, from *schifo* (“small boat”), from *skif* (“boat”), from Proto-Germanic **skipą* (“boat, ship”).

senses.definition: Easily scared or startled; timid.
senses.example: The dog likes people he knows, but he is skittish around strangers.

senses.definition: Wanton; changeable; fickle.
senses.example: Investors grew skittish, pulling money from the fund after every bad headline.

senses.definition: Difficult to manage; tricky.
senses.example: The sailboat proved skittish in the gusting wind, requiring constant attention from the crew.

core.definition: Easily frightened or startled, or nervous and jumpy, especially in animals or people in uncertain situations.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the final syllable a short, reduced 'ish', like 'ish' in 'fish'. Do not pronounce the middle 't' as a hard stop; it is a light, quick t.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use it for horses, cats and other animals that startle easily, and also for people who seem nervous, such as 'Investors are skittish after the market drop.' It is mildly informal and vivid. The word is neutral in tone, though when describing people it can suggest a lack of confidence.

distinctions.note: Nervous describes general anxiety; skittish suggests a sudden, jumpy reaction to something that might cause fright.
Timid describes a shy, cautious personality; skittish describes a reaction that can change quickly, often in response to a threat.

examples.everyday: Our new horse is pretty skittish, so don't wave anything near his face.
examples.professional: Lenders have grown skittish about commercial real estate since the rate increase.
examples.analytical: The text's skittish treatment of doctrine reveals an author more afraid of error than committed to a clear claim.

nuance.analogy: A skittish animal is like a glass of water near the edge of a table: the slightest bump can make it spill.
nuance.etymology: From 'skit', an old word for a sudden movement, with the suffix '-ish' meaning somewhat or inclined to.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'skittish' with 'skeptical', which concerns doubt rather than fear.
Using it for a single loud noise when 'startled' is more accurate.

senses.definition: The condition of being slatternly, or of being a slattern.

core.definition: The state or quality of being slovenly, untidy or careless about appearance, housekeeping or morals.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SLAT-ern-lee-nus. Keep the flap t quick, and reduce the middle and final syllables so the -ness ending sounds short and unstressed.

nuance.connotation: Negative and judgmental; it criticizes untidiness and is rarely used today.
nuance.usage_note: 'Slatternliness' is a rare, literary word that appears mostly in older novels, criticism and historical writing. Americans would not use it in conversation. In modern speech, they would say 'sloppiness,' 'messiness' or 'untidiness.' Like 'slattern,' the word carries an old gendered judgment.

distinctions.note: 'Sloppiness' is the everyday modern word for carelessness in any area; 'slatternliness' is archaic and tied to a judgment about women.
'Untidiness' is neutral and specific to disorder; 'slatternliness' adds moral disapproval.

examples.professional: The style guide recommends replacing archaic judgments like slatternliness with neutral terms such as untidiness.
examples.analytical: The Victorian novel equates domestic slatternliness with moral decline, a link the modern reader must recognize as a social construct.

nuance.analogy: Slatternliness is like an old coat in a museum: you can admire its shape, but no one wears it on a daily basis.
nuance.etymology: From 'slattern' plus '-liness'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as SLAT-ern-LEE-ness; the main stress is on the first syllable.
Using the word in modern conversation, where it sounds archaic and judgmental.

senses.definition: To reduce the volume of (music, a sound, etc.).
senses.example: The orchestra's conductor asked the brass to soft-pedal the final chord.

senses.definition: To reduce the force or impact of (something); to damp, to mute; especially, to minimize the less desirable aspects of (something); to play down, to tone down.
senses.example: The company decided to soft-pedal the layoffs in its press release.

senses.definition: To attempt to persuade someone about (something) through understatement, so that the listener accepts the good points as obvious.
senses.example: She tried to soft-pedal her argument, letting the facts make her case quietly.

senses.definition: Chiefly followed by on: to act in a less assertive or forceful manner.
senses.example: After the debate, he began to soft-pedal on his demands and asked for less.

core.definition: To play down or reduce the prominence of something, especially a problem, criticism or bad news, so it seems less serious.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SOFT, with PED-al as a weaker secondary beat ending in a syllabic l, not a full second vowel. Learners often say soft-PED-al, stressing the wrong syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when it describes lowering volume; mildly negative when it suggests evasion or hiding the truth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use soft-pedal for politicians, companies or managers who avoid controversy by downplaying bad news, as in 'The mayor soft-pedaled the budget cuts.' It can imply a deliberate, somewhat evasive choice, so it may sound critical. In music it keeps its literal sense of playing a piano more quietly with the soft pedal.

distinctions.note: Downplay is the everyday, neutral word for minimizing importance; soft-pedal suggests a more deliberate, gradual reduction of force or visibility.
Tone down describes making language, behavior or style less intense; soft-pedal is more often used for avoiding unpleasant facts or issues.
Gloss over means to hide or hurry past a problem; soft-pedal reduces its prominence while still letting it be mentioned.

examples.everyday: Dad soft-pedaled the cost of the car repair, so I didn't realize how bad it was until the bill came.
examples.professional: The vendor soft-pedaled the outage in its email, but our logs show the system was down for six hours.
examples.analytical: Commentators often soft-pedal the moral stakes of such policies, presenting them as technical adjustments rather than value choices.

nuance.analogy: Like turning down the volume on bad news while the news is still playing: everyone can still hear it, just less clearly.
nuance.etymology: From soft plus pedal; the piano's soft pedal makes the instrument play more quietly, and the figurative sense extends that idea.
common_mistakes: Stressing PED instead of SOFT: the main stress is SOFT-ped-al.
Using it to mean simply making something physically soft; the idiom is about reducing force, volume or prominence.
Adding 'on' after it, as in 'soft-pedal on the issue'; say 'soft-pedal the issue'.

soft-pedal.etymology: From *soft pedal* (“leftmost foot-pedal on most pianos which, when pushed, dampens the strings and so softens the note played”).

senses.definition: The action of solidifying.
Concentration or consolidation.
senses.example: The solidification of power in the hands of three executives worried the board members.

senses.definition: The tendency to transform an open compound into a closed compound (solid compound).
senses.example: Historians of English have documented the solidification of many open compounds into single closed words over centuries.

core.definition: The process of becoming solid, or of making something firm, fixed or stable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the -kay- syllable, and the early syllables are short and reduced. Say the -ify part as 'ih-fi', not 'ih-fy', within the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a change of state or a firming of positions, opinions or structures.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use solidification in technical contexts such as chemistry, construction and geology, and in figurative speech about opinions, alliances or power becoming fixed. In everyday talk people more often say the concrete hardened or the plan got firmer. The word sounds formal in conversation.

distinctions.note: Solidification means becoming solid, while consolidation means combining separate things into one unit.
Hardening is a general term for becoming harder, while solidification implies a complete change to a solid state or a fixed form.

examples.everyday: The concrete needs a day for solidification, so please don't park on the driveway yet.
examples.professional: The solidification of our data standards last quarter made the reporting consistent across all the teams.
examples.analytical: Historians often describe the solidification of creeds in the fourth century as a shift from open debate to fixed formulas.

nuance.analogy: Solidification is like wax cooling in a candle mold: the soft, flowing material slowly sets into a shape that holds its form.
nuance.etymology: From solidify, from Late Latin solidificare, from Latin solidus, meaning firm or whole.
common_mistakes: Confusing solidification with consolidation, which means joining things together.
Pronouncing the -ify part as 'ih-fy', which is hard to say naturally; Americans say 'ih-fih-KAY-shun' with a reduced middle.
Using it as a verb; the verb is solidify.

senses.definition: A person who believes that faith alone (as opposed to good deeds) brings salvation.
Believing, or relating to the belief, that faith alone (as opposed to good deeds) brings salvation.
senses.example: The pastor's solifidian preaching insisted that faith alone, not works, secures salvation.

core.definition: A person who believes that faith alone, not good works, brings salvation, a doctrine associated with Protestant Reformers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the FID syllable. The first syllable is a long oh sound in American speech, and the final -ian is a reduced un.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic or theological writing; can sound polemical when used by critics of Protestant teaching.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use solifidian mainly in theology classes, church history, and religious debate. Most people would say 'Protestant' or 'Lutheran' in everyday talk, and solifidian is used when discussing the specific doctrine. It can sound technical or slightly combative in conversation.

distinctions.note: Protestant is a broad church identity; solifidian names a person defined by a particular doctrine about faith and justification.
Sola fide is the Latin doctrine itself; solifidian is the person or adjective describing someone holding it.

examples.everyday: At Bible study my friend said he was a solifidian, and we spent the evening talking about grace.
examples.professional: In our seminary class, the professor explained why a solifidian reading of Romans changed how the Reformers preached.
examples.analytical: A solifidian account of justification separates the declaration of righteousness from any moral transformation that must follow.

nuance.analogy: A solifidian is like a traveler who says the ticket alone gets you on the train; the ticket is everything, though the trip still shapes the traveler.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sola fides, faith alone, plus the suffix -ian.
common_mistakes: Confusing solifidian with solipsism, which means belief that only the self exists.
Pronouncing the first syllable as 'SOL' with a short vowel; in American speech it is closer to 'soh-l'.
nuance.biblical_note: The key Greek words are pistis (faith, trust) and dikaioo (to justify, to declare or make righteous). Romans 3:28 says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Galatians 2:16 says a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. James 2:24 says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone, which is why the debate matters.

traditions.view: Orthodox teaching stresses faith as the beginning of salvation, joined with love, sacraments, and cooperation with grace. Orthodox theologians generally reject the claim that faith alone, apart from transformation, is sufficient.

Catholic teaching holds that justification involves faith together with grace-enabled works, and the Council of Trent rejected the view that faith alone justifies. Catholics affirm that faith must be living and expressed in charity.

Protestants generally affirm justification by faith alone as central to the Reformation. Lutherans and Reformed Christians emphasize it strongly, while many Anglicans and Baptists affirm it with variations on how faith relates to sanctification and works.

senses.definition: To make (something) less innocent or natural; to artificialize.
To make (something) more sophisticated (“complex, developed, or refined”); to develop, to refine.
To make (oneself or someone) more sophisticated (“experienced in the ways of the world, that is, cosmopolitan or worldly-wise”); to cosmopolitanize.

To alter and make impure (something) by mixing it with some foreign or inferior substance, especially with an intention to deceive; to adulterate; to corrupt or deceive (someone, their thinking, etc.).
To change the meaning of (something) in a deceptive or misleading way.
To practice sophistry (“the (deliberate) making of arguments that seem plausible but are fallacious or misleading”).

core.definition: To make something more complex or refined, or to make someone more worldly, experienced and cultured.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, suh-FIS-tih-kayt. The first syllable is a weak schwa, and the final 'ate' is a long 'ayt' sound, not 'it'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use sophisticate as a verb in everyday speech; they usually say make more sophisticated or refine. The verb appears in literary criticism, business writing and academic prose. Its tone can be neutral or negative, depending on whether the change is good or artificial.

distinctions.note: Refine suggests making something purer or better; sophisticate can also mean making something more artificial or complicated.
Sophisticated is an adjective; sophisticate is a verb meaning the act of making something or someone more sophisticated.

examples.everyday: Don't sophisticate the recipe too much; plain salt and lemon is all it needs.
examples.professional: We shouldn't sophisticate the model before we have a baseline, or we won't know which change helped.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that modern marketing sophisticates desire until it looks like authentic taste.

nuance.analogy: To sophisticate something is like adding gears to a bicycle: it becomes more capable, but it may also become harder to repair.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin sophisticare, 'to adulterate', from Greek sophizein, 'to make wise'.
common_mistakes: Using sophisticate as a noun for a sophisticated person; the noun is sophisticate only in the sense of a worldly person.
Confusing the verb sophisticate with the adjective sophisticated in everyday sentences.

senses.definition: A narrow strip running down a movie film that carries the recorded sound in synchronization with the pictures.
senses.example: The projectionist checked that the soundtrack on the reel was clean and in sync.

senses.definition: The sound (especially the music) component of a movie, video game, etc.
A recording or compilation of recordings of such music for sale.
senses.example: I bought the soundtrack to the movie the same night and played it on the drive home.

senses.definition: A background sound that is part of a larger event.
senses.example: The soundtrack of the city, with sirens and car horns, filled the apartment all night.

senses.definition: Popular music associated with a particular historical era or time of one's life, especially nostalgically.
senses.example: the soundtrack of our relationship

senses.definition: To provide, or to act as, the sound or music component of a film.
senses.example: The composer agreed to soundtrack the indie film for a modest fee and a share of profits.

core.definition: The recorded music and sound effects that accompany a movie, TV show, or video game, or the album of that music.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'tr' is pronounced with an American retroflex r, and the vowel in 'track' is the short 'a' of cat.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a standard descriptive word in entertainment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use soundtrack for both the music in a movie and the album sold separately. In casual speech someone might say 'the soundtrack is amazing' about a movie's music. It can also be used as a verb, meaning to provide the music for a film.

distinctions.note: A score is music written specifically for a film, usually instrumental; a soundtrack can include existing songs as well.
A theme song is one recurring tune associated with a show; a soundtrack is the whole collection of music.

examples.everyday: Have you heard the soundtrack from that new Marvel movie? It's really good.
examples.professional: The marketing team wants the soundtrack released on streaming platforms before the film premieres.
examples.analytical: The film's soundtrack functions as a second narrative, using repeated motifs to signal shifts in the protagonist's memory.

nuance.analogy: Like the background music in a grocery store, but built deliberately to shape how you feel about every scene on screen.
nuance.etymology: From sound and track, the original name for the strip of film carrying the recorded sound.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'sound-track' with a strong stop; in speech the two words are linked into one smooth word.
Using it to mean just the musical score; a soundtrack can include songs by other artists.

conversation.text: The soundtrack is amazing; I've been listening to it all week.
I bought the soundtrack after seeing the movie.
That song was on the soundtrack of my childhood.

senses.definition: A health resort near a mineral spring or hot spring.
senses.example: After the long hike, we relaxed at a spa built around a natural hot spring.

senses.definition: A trendy or fashionable resort.
senses.example: Everyone in the city wants to be seen at the trendy spa in Aspen this summer.

senses.definition: A health club.
senses.example: They went to a spa for a massage.

senses.definition: A hot tub.
senses.example: Their bath is fitted with a spa.

senses.definition: A convenience store.
senses.example: I stopped at the corner spa to grab milk and a bag of ice.

core.definition: A place offering massages, facials and other treatments for relaxation and health, often at a hotel or resort.

pronunciation.tip: Use the open, unrounded vowel of 'father' and 'hot', which is the same vowel in General American. Do not say 'spay' with a long a sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests relaxation and self-care, though day spas can be expensive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'spa' for day spas, hotel spas and wellness centers offering massages and body treatments. In some contexts, 'nail spa' or 'med spa' refers to a place with specific services, so check what is offered. Typical replies include 'Did you treat yourself?' or 'That sounds amazing, how was it?'

distinctions.note: A salon mainly does hair, nails and styling, while a spa focuses on relaxation treatments such as massages and facials.
A resort is a larger hotel complex with many amenities, and a spa may be just one part of it.
A sauna is a heated room for sweating, while a spa may offer saunas along with other treatments.

examples.everyday: Let's book a spa day for your birthday; they do a great facial there.
examples.professional: Our company offsite includes a spa package, so we should confirm the room block with the hotel's events team.
examples.analytical: The modern spa, once tied to healing waters, now sells experience and self-care as a product.

nuance.analogy: A spa visit works like a system reboot for the body: it clears out the stress and lets you run more smoothly afterward.
nuance.etymology: Named after Spa, a town in Belgium famous for its mineral springs.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I went to spa' without the article; say 'I went to a spa' or 'I went to the spa'.
Pronouncing it 'spay' with a long a sound, which sounds like a different word.

spa.etymology: The term is derived from the name of the Belgian town of Spa, where since medieval times illnesses caused by iron deficiency were treated by drinking chalybeate spring water.

senses.definition: To communicate with one's voice, to say words out loud.
senses.example: I was so surprised I couldn't speak.

senses.definition: To have a conversation.
senses.example: It's been ages since we've spoken.

senses.definition: To communicate or converse by some means other than orally, such as writing or facial expressions.
senses.example: He spoke of it in his diary.

senses.definition: To deliver a message to a group; to deliver a speech.
senses.example: This evening I shall speak on the topic of correct English usage.

senses.definition: To be able to communicate in a language.
senses.example: He speaks Mandarin fluently.

senses.definition: To be able to communicate in the manner of specialists in a field.
To utter.
senses.example: I was so surprised that I couldn't speak a word.

senses.definition: To communicate (some fact or feeling); to bespeak, to indicate.
To understand (as though it were a language).
senses.example: Sorry, I don't speak idiot.

senses.definition: To produce a sound; to sound.
Of a bird, to be able to vocally reproduce words or phrases from a human language.
Language, jargon, or terminology used uniquely in a particular environment or group.
senses.example: corporate speak; IT speak

senses.definition: Speech, conversation. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
Clipping of speaker point.
senses.example: We will deduct speaks for hesitation.

senses.definition: (dated) A low class bar, a speakeasy.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To say words aloud in order to communicate, or to talk in a particular language.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a long ee vowel. Keep the final k sharp, and do not add an extra vowel, such as 'speak-uh'. Be careful not to confuse it with 'speech', which has a different final consonant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is used in every context, from casual talk to formal speeches.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say speak for talking aloud and for knowing a language, as in 'Do you speak Spanish?' For ordinary conversation, Americans often prefer talk, but speak sounds more formal or deliberate in phrases like 'speak to the manager' or 'speak up'. The natural reply to 'Do you speak English?' is 'A little' or 'Yes, a bit'. In a polite request, 'Could you speak more slowly?' is friendly and natural.

distinctions.note: Talk is the more casual and frequent word in everyday American speech, while speak can sound more formal or deliberate.
Say focuses on the specific words used, while speak focuses on the act of producing speech or using a language.

examples.everyday: Could you speak a little louder? I can't hear you over the TV.
examples.professional: Before we vote, I'd like to speak briefly about the risk to the timeline.
examples.analytical: Wittgenstein argued that we cannot speak meaningfully about what lies beyond the limits of language.

nuance.analogy: To speak is like opening a faucet: the words flow out, and the listener collects them.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sprecan, meaning to speak, from a Germanic root.
common_mistakes: Adding a preposition when speaking a language: say 'I speak English', not 'I speak to English'.
Confusing speak and speech in pronunciation; speak ends with a k sound, speech ends with ch.

speak.etymology: From Middle English *speke*, *speken* (“to speak”), from Old English *specan* (“to speak”).

senses.definition: A long stick with a sharp tip used as a weapon for throwing or thrusting, or anything used to make a thrusting motion.
A lance with barbed prongs, used by fishermen to retrieve fish.
senses.example: The old fisherman raised his spear and waited for the salmon to pass below.

senses.definition: An illegal maneuver using the end of a hockey stick to strike into another hockey player.
senses.example: The referee penalized him for a spear after he jabbed the opponent in the gut.

senses.definition: In professional wrestling, a running tackle in which the wrestler's shoulder is driven into the opponent's midsection.
senses.example: The challenger hit the champion with a spear that drove them both into the mat.

senses.definition: A shoot, as of grass; a spire.
senses.example: After the spring rains, a green spear of grass pushed through the frozen soil.

senses.definition: The feather of a horse.
senses.example: The farrier trimmed the long spear of white hair above the horse's hooves before the show.

senses.definition: The rod to which the bucket, or plunger, of a pump is attached; a pump rod.
senses.example: The mechanic replaced the worn spear in the well pump before winter set in.

senses.definition: A long, thin strip from a vegetable.
senses.example: asparagus and broccoli spears

senses.definition: The sprout of a plant, stalk.
senses.example: A tender spear of asparagus poked up through the mulch by early April.

senses.definition: (historical) A soldier armed with such a weapon; a spearman.
senses.example: The Swiss army hired a line of spears to hold the bridge against the cavalry.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To pierce with a spear.
senses.example: The hunter speared a salmon in the shallows with one clean thrust.

senses.definition: To penetrate or strike with, or as if with, any long narrow object; to make a thrusting motion that catches an object on the tip of a long device.
senses.example: She speared an olive from the jar with a long fork and dropped it on her plate.

senses.definition: To tackle an opponent by ramming into them with one's helmet.
senses.example: The linebacker speared the running back with his helmet, and the referee threw a flag.

senses.definition: To shoot into a long stem, as some plants do.
senses.example: Once the lettuce started to spear in the heat, we pulled every plant.

senses.definition: Male.
senses.example: a spear counterpart

senses.definition: Pertaining to male family members.
senses.example: the spear side of the family

core.definition: A long pole with a sharp point at one end, used for throwing or thrusting, especially in hunting or war.

pronunciation.tip: Use a clear American rhotic r at the end of 'speer', pronounced with the tongue curled back. Keep the vowel short, like 'ih', and do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it describes a weapon or tool, and in Scripture it often carries a sense of conflict or danger.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spear mostly when talking about history, hunting, sports, or literature. Everyday speech rarely needs it, but it appears in phrases about fishing and in biblical or historical discussions. For a modern weapon, Americans would say 'rifle' or 'gun', not spear.

distinctions.note: A lance is a long weapon used by a mounted knight in charging. A spear can be thrown or held by someone on foot.
A javelin is a light spear thrown in athletic competition. A spear is a broader term for the weapon in war or hunting.

examples.everyday: My grandfather brought back a fishing spear from his trip to Alaska.
examples.professional: The museum exhibit includes a bronze spear point from the early Iron Age.
examples.analytical: In the narrative, the spear becomes a symbol of violence that the text then reframes through the cross.

nuance.analogy: A spear is like a long, pointed stick that becomes a weapon the moment you throw it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English spere, a pole or spear, of Germanic origin.
common_mistakes: Using spear for a modern gun or rifle in everyday conversation.
Pronouncing it 'spee-ar' with two full syllables; it is one syllable in American speech.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible the usual word is chanit, a spear or lance, and the Greek New Testament uses logchē, a lance or spear. Spears appear in battle, in court intrigue, and in the passion narrative. In 1 Samuel 18:10-11 King Saul hurls a spear at David, twice, and misses, showing jealousy and danger. In 1 Samuel 17:7 Goliath's spear has a shaft like a weaver's beam and a head weighing six hundred shekels of iron, emphasizing the strength of the Philistine champion. In John 19:34 a soldier pierces the side of the crucified Jesus with a spear, a detail that the Gospel uses as a sign of his death.

spear.etymology: From Middle English *spere*, *sperre*, *spear*, from Old English *spere*, from **speru*, from Proto-Germanic **speru*, from Proto-Indo-European **sperH-*.

senses.definition: Distinguished by a unique, particular, or unusual quality.
senses.example: a special episode of a television series

senses.definition: Of particular value or interest; dear; beloved.
senses.example: Everyone is special to someone.

senses.definition: Constituting or relating to a species.
senses.example: Having seven dark spots is a special property unique to Coccinella septempunctata.

senses.definition: Of or related to disabilities, especially learning or intellectual disabilities.
senses.example: special education, special needs

senses.definition: Stupid, lacking intelligence.
senses.example: What do you mean, you don't understand the sign? What are you, special?

senses.definition: Of, being, or pertaining to sexual intercourse or the genitals.
senses.example: The parents told the kids not to bother them during special time.

senses.definition: Infused with a drug, especially marijuana; being an edible.
senses.example: The bakery sold special brownies, and one bite left me giggling for an hour.

senses.definition: Of or related to unconventional warfare.
senses.example: special forces, special operations

senses.definition: Appointed specifically to examine a single event or issue.
senses.example: For the few times the U.S. Supreme Court has to actually try a case, they will appoint a special master to do so.

senses.definition: A reduction in consumer cost (usually for a limited time) for items or services rendered; the thing thus sold.
senses.example: We're running a special on turkey for Thanksgiving.

senses.definition: A meal offered only at a certain time by a restaurant, not as a standing fixture of the menu; often, one of a rotation of meals systematically offered for a lower price; also often a dish at a nondiscounted price that is seasonal or otherwise exciting or unusual.
senses.example: Today's dinner special is wild salmon, which we don't normally get a chance to offer.

senses.definition: Unusual or exceptional episode of a series.
senses.example: Did you see the Christmas special?

senses.definition: Anything that is not according to normal practice, plan, or schedule, as an unscheduled run of transportation that is normally scheduled.
senses.example: Thousands came to see the special that carried the President's coffin.

senses.definition: Any unlicensed medicine produced or obtained for a specific individual patient.
senses.example: My cousin's doctor obtained a special from overseas because the approved treatment was too expensive.

senses.definition: An award, typically a free game, that is made available to the player upon reaching or completing a major objective in a pinball game.
senses.example: He racked up enough points to earn a special, which gave him a free game.

senses.definition: A journalist sent to the scene of an event to report back.
senses.example: The network sent a special to cover the hurricane's landfall along the Gulf Coast.

senses.definition: A dispatch sent back by a special correspondent.
senses.example: Her special from the border town ran on the front page this morning.

senses.definition: A light that illuminates a specific person or thing on the stage.
senses.example: The lighting designer aimed a special at the singer during her solo.

senses.definition: One of certain mixed-breed dogs.
senses.example: Singapore Special; Darwin special

senses.definition: A racehorse predicted to win; a sure thing.
senses.example: Everyone at the track bet heavily on the favorite, calling it a special.

senses.definition: To supervise a patient one-on-one.
senses.example: The nurse agreed to special the suicidal patient until the psychiatrist arrived.

core.definition: Different from what is usual or ordinary, having a unique quality, purpose, or importance that sets something apart.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'ci' in 'special' sounds like 'sh', so it is not 'spe-shee-al'. The final syllable is a reduced vowel followed by l, so it sounds like 'uhl' rather than 'ahl'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests something valued, out of the ordinary, or emotionally meaningful, though 'special' can sound vague or patronizing if used to describe someone's unusual needs or abilities.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'special' constantly in everyday life, for example 'Is there anything special today?' at a restaurant, or 'a special day' for a birthday. Americans also use 'special' in a sense of a limited-time deal or menu item. In some contexts, such as 'special education' or 'special needs', the word is standard but should be used respectfully.

distinctions.note: Special describes a quality something has, while especially means particularly or more than usual, as in 'I especially like this one.'
Unique means one of a kind, while special means distinctive or important, so something can be special without being unique.

examples.everyday: Is there anything special on the menu tonight, or should I just order the usual?
examples.professional: We need a special approval from the security team before we can deploy this change to production.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguishes a special virtue from a general one, and that distinction helps explain how particular excellences fit into the whole of a good life.

nuance.analogy: A special day is like a single lit candle in a dark room: it stands out from the ordinary background around it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin specialis, of a particular kind, from species.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'ci' as 'see' or 'shee', rather than the 'sh' sound in 'spesh-uhl'.
Using 'special' to mean 'especially' in sentences like 'I like it, special the dessert.'
Saying 'very special' with a limited sense when Americans usually say 'really special' or simply 'special' in everyday talk.

special.etymology: From Middle English **special*, *especial*, *especiall*, from Old French *especial*, from Latin *speciālis* (from *speciēs*).

senses.definition: The condition of being spectacular.

core.definition: The quality of being impressive, dramatic, or extraordinary to see.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the 'lair' syllable, with secondary stress on 'tak'. The 't' in the middle of 'ih-tee' is a quick flap, so it sounds like a soft 'd'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes the dramatic quality of something, sometimes with a hint of exaggeration.
nuance.usage_note: This is a rare, formal noun that Americans seldom use in conversation. They say 'how spectacular it is' or 'the spectacular quality of' in ordinary speech. You might encounter it in art criticism, sports writing, or academic prose about visual media.

distinctions.note: Spectacle is a concrete impressive sight or event, while spectacularity is the abstract quality that makes something spectacular.
Splendor stresses beauty and magnificence, while spectacularity stresses the dramatic, attention-grabbing quality.

examples.professional: Marketing wants more spectacularity in the product launch, so we should add a live demo.
examples.analytical: The critic argues that the film's spectacularity masks a thin narrative, as dazzling visuals replace emotional development.

nuance.analogy: Spectacularity is the glow of a stage light: the quality that makes everything in the spotlight stand out.
nuance.etymology: From spectacular, from Latin spectaculum, a sight, plus the noun suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in spec-TAC-yoo-lar-ity, instead of spek-tak-yuh-LAIR-ih-tee.
Using it in everyday speech where the adjective spectacular is more natural.

senses.definition: To twist one's body with snakelike motions.
senses.example: The prisoner managed to squirm out of the straitjacket.

senses.definition: To twist in discomfort, especially from shame or embarrassment.
senses.example: I recounted the embarrassing story in detail just to watch him squirm.

senses.definition: To evade a question, an interviewer etc. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The senator tried to squirm out of the reporter's question about the missing funds.

senses.definition: A twisting, snakelike movement of the body.
senses.example: The toddler gave a squirm and wriggled free from his mother's arms.

core.definition: To twist and wriggle the body, especially from discomfort, shame or embarrassment; also to evade a question awkwardly.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a strong r-colored vowel. Do not add an extra vowel like 'skuh-wurm', and keep the final m closed.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use squirm for a child who cannot sit still in church or a school assembly, and for an adult who feels embarrassed during a meeting or a compliment. The sense of evading a question is common in US news and politics, usually with 'squirm out of' or 'squirm around'. The word is usually sympathetic or humorous rather than harsh.

distinctions.note: Wriggle is often playful or small-scale, like a worm or toes moving, while squirm more often suggests discomfort or embarrassment.
Fidget means small, restless hand or foot movements, often from boredom or nerves, while squirm involves the whole body twisting.
Writhe suggests intense pain or agony and is a much stronger word than squirm.

examples.everyday: Our toddler squirmed through the whole Thanksgiving prayer, so we ended up leaving early.
examples.professional: When the VP asked why the release slipped, the project lead squirmed and gave a vague answer about dependencies.
examples.analytical: The essay squirms under its own premise, since it assumes the conclusion it claims to establish.

nuance.analogy: Like a worm on a hook, the body squirms when it cannot find a comfortable position.
common_mistakes: Using squirm for one small movement; it describes repeated twisting of the body
Saying 'squirm from' a question instead of the more natural 'squirm out of' a question

senses.definition: An instrument from which a liquid is forcefully ejected in a small, quick stream.
A small, quick stream; a jet.
senses.example: a squirt of body lotion

senses.definition: The whole system of flow in the vicinity of a source.
senses.example: The hydrologist measured the squirt near the spring to see how the seepage spread downstream.

senses.definition: A burst of noise.
senses.example: A sudden squirt of static from the radio startled everyone in the quiet kitchen.

senses.definition: An annoyingly pretentious person; a whippersnapper.
senses.example: Nobody at the faculty party took the cocky young squirt seriously.

senses.definition: A small child.
senses.example: Hey squirt! Where you been?

senses.definition: Female ejaculate.
senses.example: The sexual health textbook explained squirting as a distinct phenomenon separate from urination.

senses.definition: An act of urination.
senses.example: Excuse me, I need to take a squirt.

senses.definition: A maneuver in which a kayak is forced into a nearly vertical position.
senses.example: Her first squirt in the rapids left her kayak standing almost straight up on its tail.

senses.definition: To be thrown out, or ejected, in a rapid stream, from a narrow orifice.
senses.example: The toothpaste squirted from the tube.

senses.definition: To cause to be ejected, in a rapid stream, from a narrow orifice.
senses.example: Squeeze the bottle gently so the lemon juice squirts out in a thin stream.

senses.definition: To emit, eject, or excrete (something).
senses.example: The startled skunk squirted a foul spray from its scent glands.

senses.definition: To hit with a rapid stream of liquid.
senses.example: My little brother squirted me with the garden hose again.

senses.definition: To ejaculate.
To forcefully maneuver against the current so that the end of a kayak is forced nearly vertical.
senses.example: He learned to squirt his kayak across the eddy line without capsizing.

senses.definition: To 3D print (a firearm, or a part thereof).
senses.example: Investigators found the suspect had used a home printer to squirt a plastic handgun.

core.definition: A short, forceful spurt of liquid; as a verb, to eject liquid in a rapid, narrow stream from a small opening.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a strong r-colored vowel, followed by a clear t. Do not add a vowel between the sounds, like 'skuh-wert'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'squirt some ketchup' or 'squirt a little lemon on it' in casual cooking and dining, and 'squirt gun' for a children's toy. Calling someone a 'little squirt' is an affectionate but sometimes teasing way to describe a small child. Squirt sounds informal, so in formal writing Americans would more often say 'spray' or 'eject'.

distinctions.note: Spray means a wider mist of fine droplets, while squirt means a narrow, focused stream.
Spurt means a sudden burst, often of energy or flow, and is more general than the narrow stream of squirt.
Spritz means a light mist, usually from a small bottle, and sounds more casual or fashionable than squirt.

examples.everyday: Can you squirt a little more ketchup on my fries before they get cold?
examples.professional: Can you squirt the revised numbers to the whole team before the 10 a.m. call?
examples.analytical: The sample is ejected in a squirt rather than a steady flow, which explains the sharp pressure spikes in the readings.

nuance.analogy: Like a water pistol, a squirt is a quick, narrow jet that stops as soon as the pressure is released.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a squirt of the lemon' when the natural phrase is 'a squirt of lemon juice'
Confusing squirt with spurt, which describes a sudden burst rather than a narrow stream

squirt.etymology: From Middle English *squirten,squyrten*, of uncertain origin; probably.

senses.definition: Of an event, intentionally performed while being falsely contrived to appear authentic or coincidental.
senses.example: The car accident was actually staged so he could collect the insurance money.

senses.definition: Intended for the stage as in a theater.
senses.example: The staged performance was good, but I liked the book better.

core.definition: Deliberately arranged or performed to look spontaneous, real, or accidental, though it is not.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on STAYJ, and the final -ed is a d sound after a voiced consonant, so it is one syllable. Many learners add an extra syllable and say STAY-jed.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests a fake or manipulated event, often designed to deceive viewers or the public.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use staged in news, politics, and social media to say that a photo, protest, or event was arranged for effect. In a theater context, a staged reading simply means presented on stage, which is neutral. Calling something staged often implies that the audience is being fooled, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Fake means not real in any sense; staged specifically means arranged to look spontaneous, often before an audience or camera.
Scripted means following a written plan, which may be honest; staged implies a false impression of spontaneity.

examples.everyday: That photo of the lake looks too perfect; I bet it was staged.
examples.professional: The team flagged the demo as staged, since the sensor data was edited before the presentation.
examples.analytical: A reality show that appears unscripted may still be staged, which raises questions about what viewers are really seeing.

nuance.analogy: Like a movie set built to look like a real street, it appears authentic only from the angle the camera chooses.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of stage, from Old French estage.
common_mistakes: Using staged to mean any fake object; it refers to deliberate arrangement to create a false impression, often of spontaneity.
Pronouncing the -ed as a separate syllable, as in STAY-jed.

senses.definition: A restaurant that specializes in good cuts of meat, particularly steak.
senses.example: We celebrated her promotion at a downtown steakhouse with dry-aged ribeyes and a great wine list.

core.definition: A restaurant that specializes in high-quality beef steaks and usually serves them with sides.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'STAYK.' The second syllable 'house' is one word with a secondary stress, so say it quickly and don't split it into two separate words.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a classic, hearty American dinner, often a bit upscale.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say steakhouse for both casual and fancy restaurants that focus on steak. You might hear 'Let's go to a steakhouse for Dad's birthday.' Steakhouses are often dark, with red meat, big portions, and classic sides like baked potatoes and creamed spinach.

distinctions.note: A grill is a cooking device or a casual restaurant; a steakhouse is specifically about steak.
A bistro is a small, casual French-style restaurant; a steakhouse focuses on beef and is usually larger.
A chophouse specializes in chops, while a steakhouse specializes in steaks; both are classic American dining.

examples.everyday: Let's go to that steakhouse downtown for your birthday; they have great ribeyes.
examples.professional: Our client dinner is booked at a steakhouse near the office, so please arrive by seven.
examples.analytical: The steakhouse as a dining form reflects American ideas about abundance and masculine hospitality.

nuance.analogy: Like a sports bar for beef lovers, built around one main attraction.
nuance.etymology: From steak (from Old Norse steik) plus house, a place of service.
common_mistakes: Saying 'steak house' as two words in formal writing, when the standard form is 'steakhouse.'
Pronouncing the 'ea' as a short e instead of the long a sound in 'steak.'

conversation.text: For his birthday, we took Dad to a nice steakhouse.
That steakhouse is pricey, but the steaks are incredible.
Is there a steakhouse near the hotel? The client loves steak.

senses.definition: To leave secretively.

core.definition: To leave quietly and secretly, often without being noticed by others.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on WAY, with secondary stress on steal. Reduce 'a' to a quick schwa and link the words smoothly: 'steel-uh-WAY'. The word 'steal' sounds the same as 'steel'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly playful: it suggests a quiet, deliberate exit, sometimes with a sense of mischief or longing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use steal away in narratives, personal stories, and casual speech, especially when someone wants to leave quietly for a nap, a break, or a moment alone. It is less common than sneak out, and it sounds softer and slightly more literary. A natural reply is 'Go ahead, I'll cover for you.'

distinctions.note: Sneak out is more informal and often suggests avoiding trouble, while steal away has a softer, sometimes nostalgic or poetic tone.
Slip away emphasizes an easy, unnoticed departure, while steal away implies more deliberate secrecy.

examples.everyday: I'm going to steal away for a quick nap before dinner.
examples.professional: She stole away from the meeting early without telling anyone on the team.
examples.analytical: The narrator steals away at dawn, leaving the household asleep and the debt unresolved.

nuance.analogy: Like a cat slipping out of the room when no one is watching.
nuance.etymology: Steal from Old English stelan, meaning to take secretly; away from Old English aweg.
common_mistakes: Using steal away with an object, as in 'steal away the car' instead of 'steal the car'.
Confusing it with 'steel away', which is a spelling error since the words sound identical.

senses.definition: To dominate a performance through charisma, humor or powerful acting.

core.definition: To attract more attention and admiration than the main performers, through charisma, humor or powerful acting.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SCENE, the last word, while STEAL keeps a weaker secondary stress and THE reduces to a quick thuh. Say the phrase as one smooth stream so it sounds like steel-thuh-SEEN, not three separate words.

nuance.connotation: Positive and admiring. It praises someone who outshines the others, though it can hint that the star overshadowed the main act.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this about actors, comedians, speakers, or even a kid at a family event, usually to praise a memorable moment. It is informal and very common in movie reviews, group chats, and casual conversation. A natural reply is 'Totally, she was hilarious' or 'He really did.'

distinctions.note: Nearly identical in meaning, but steal the scene refers to one scene or moment in a film or play, while steal the show covers the whole event.
Upstage implies deliberately drawing attention away from another performer, often with a negative sense, while steal the scene is an admiring description of success.

collocations: steal the scene with a one-liner
steal the scene in the movie

examples.everyday: Did you see the dog in that commercial? He totally stole the scene.
examples.professional: Our new analyst stole the scene at the quarterly review with a clear chart that explained the churn data.
examples.analytical: In the novel, the minor character's monologue steals the scene from the hero and shifts the reader's sympathy toward a rival moral vision.

nuance.analogy: Like a backup singer who gets the loudest applause at a concert, even though the headliner is still on stage.
nuance.etymology: Steal comes from Old English stelan; scene comes from Greek skēnē, meaning tent or stage building.
common_mistakes: Dropping the article and saying 'steal scene'; the idiom requires 'the'.
Using the idiom for literal theft or a bad moment; it always signals admiring success.

senses.definition: Used to decrease the secondary voltage relative to the primary voltage.
senses.example: The stepdown transformer on the pole reduces 7200 volts to 240 for the house.

senses.definition: A gradual reduction.

core.definition: A gradual reduction in size, level, amount or rank, often a move to something less than before.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, STEP, and the second syllable is a secondary stress with the American ow sound. Do not drop the d, and do not stress the second syllable more than the first.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it often implies that something has declined in quality or status.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stepdown in business, health care and everyday talk about moving to a smaller or less prestigious place, such as 'Moving to the condo was a stepdown.' In hospitals, a step-down unit is for patients who need less intensive care than the ICU. Electrically, it refers to a transformer that lowers voltage.

distinctions.note: Decrease is a neutral, general word; stepdown suggests a series of reductions or a move to a lower level.
Downgrade is more negative and often official; stepdown can be a neutral or planned reduction.

collocations: a stepdown from the old job

examples.everyday: Moving from the big house to a smaller condo was a real stepdown, but we like the simpler life.
examples.professional: The team planned a stepdown in server capacity once the holiday traffic ended, to cut cloud costs.
examples.analytical: The shift of authority from national agencies to local boards represents a stepdown in institutional power, not merely a reorganization.

nuance.analogy: Like walking down a staircase one level at a time rather than dropping straight to the bottom.
nuance.etymology: From the verb step down, combining step (Old English stæppan) and down (Old English dūn).
common_mistakes: Writing a step down as a noun phrase when you mean a closed noun; both forms exist, but the closed stepdown is used for the reduction.
Confusing stepdown with promotion; it is the opposite of a step up.

senses.definition: Having a pungent smell.
Very bad and undesirable.
senses.example: I have a stinking cold.

senses.definition: Very drunk.
An intensifier, a hypallage.
senses.example: We don’t need your stinking sympathy.

senses.definition: The emission of a foul smell.
senses.example: The stinking from the sewer drains filled the whole alley by noon.

core.definition: Having a very strong, unpleasant smell; informally, also used to mean very bad or very drunk.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the ng sound clear, without adding a hard g after it. Do not confuse it with stinging, which sounds similar but means something else.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a strong bad smell, and the intensifier uses such as stinking rich are casual and can sound crude or rude when applied to a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stinking for things with a strong bad smell, like a trash can or gym socks, often in an annoyed or joking tone. As an intensifier, stinking rich and stinking drunk are common in casual speech. In formal writing, use malodorous or foul-smelling instead.

distinctions.note: Stinky is more casual and often used by children or parents; stinking is stronger and can carry disgust or anger.
Smelly is the neutral everyday word and can be mild, while stinking means the smell is very strong.

examples.everyday: Throw that milk out, it's stinking up the fridge.
examples.professional: The conference room is stinking of burnt coffee, so can facilities come take a look before the meeting?
examples.analytical: The report is stinking of bias, since every counterexample is dismissed without argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a gym bag left in a closed car, the smell reaches you before you see the source.
nuance.etymology: From stink plus the -ing suffix; Old English stincan meant to emit a smell.
common_mistakes: Confusing stinking (smelling bad) with stingy (unwilling to spend money).
Using stinking as a neutral word for any smell; it means strong and bad, so it is rude to say about food someone cooked for you.

stinking.etymology: From Middle English *stynkynge*, *stinkinge*, *stinkinde*, *stinkende*, *stynkande*, *stynkand*, from Old English *stincende*, from Proto-Germanic **stinkwandz* (“stinking”), present participle of Proto-Germanic **stinkwaną* (“to stink”), equivalent to…

senses.definition: Fine work done by stitching.

core.definition: Decorative needlework, such as embroidery or appliqué, done by hand with stitches.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The ending '-ery' is a reduced schwa plus a rhotic 'ree,' so it sounds like 'uh-ree,' not 'ur-ee' with full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests craft, creativity and handmade quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stitchery' for decorative hand needlework, often in crafts, home decor or hobby groups. It is less common than 'embroidery' and 'needlework' but appears in craft stores, art classes and wall hangings. Using it for ordinary sewing or repairs sounds odd.

distinctions.note: Embroidery is a specific technique of decorating fabric with thread, while stitchery is a broader word for decorative stitched work.
Needlework is the broadest term for any work done with a needle, including mending and knitting, while stitchery is more decorative.

examples.everyday: My sister took a stitchery class at the library, and now she makes little wall hangings.
examples.professional: The gift shop sells handmade stitchery from local artists, so we can feature it in the spring catalog.
examples.analytical: Stitchery records the maker's time and attention, which is why museums treat it as a serious art form.

nuance.analogy: Like painting with thread: each stitch adds a little color and texture to the cloth.
nuance.etymology: From stitch (noun) plus -ery, a suffix meaning 'work of a kind.'
common_mistakes: Using it for simple sewing or mending, where 'sewing' is the normal word.
Stressing the last syllable, as in 'stitch-ER-ee.'

senses.definition: Random, randomly determined.

core.definition: Involving randomness; determined by chance and described using probability rather than fixed rules.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, KAS. Many learners stress the first syllable or pronounce the ch-like sound as a k, but the stress is the key feature.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is precise and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stochastic mainly in mathematics, statistics, data science and engineering, rather than in everyday talk. It is often paired with process or model. Using it in a team meeting is natural, but in casual conversation people usually say random or probabilistic instead.

distinctions.note: Random is everyday and general, while stochastic is technical and implies a process governed by probability.
Probabilistic emphasizes that outcomes are described by probabilities, while stochastic emphasizes the presence of random variation over time.

examples.everyday: My weather app uses a stochastic model, so the forecast can change a little each time I refresh it.
examples.professional: We should use a stochastic simulation here, since the customer arrival times are not fixed.
examples.analytical: A stochastic account of evolution treats variation as genuinely chancy rather than as hidden design.

nuance.analogy: Like rolling dice: you can predict the average outcome, but not each individual roll.
nuance.etymology: From Greek stochastikos, skillful at aiming, from stochazesthai, to aim at.
common_mistakes: Using stochastic to mean stochastic as a casual synonym for strange, when it means random in a probabilistic sense.
Stressing the first syllable as STOH-kas-tik.

stochastic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *στοχαστικός*, from *στοχάζομαι* (“aim at a target, guess”), from *στόχος* (“an aim, a guess”).

senses.definition: Gastroenteritis.
senses.example: I caught stomach flu from my daughter and spent the whole weekend in bed.

core.definition: A contagious viral illness causing nausea, vomiting and diarrhea. It is not influenza, though people casually use the word flu for it.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun, the stress falls on stomach, with flu as a weaker second element. Keep the schwa in the middle of stomach clear and short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it describes an unpleasant but common and temporary illness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say stomach flu or stomach bug for illnesses like norovirus that cause vomiting and diarrhea, usually for a day or two. Doctors call it gastroenteritis, and the word flu alone usually means influenza. People say they have the stomach flu when they miss work or school, and a typical reply is 'Feel better soon.'

distinctions.note: Influenza is a respiratory virus causing fever, cough and body aches, while stomach flu affects the digestive tract.
Food poisoning comes from contaminated food or drink, which can be bacterial or toxic, while stomach flu is usually a viral infection spread person to person.

collocations: a bad case of stomach flu

examples.everyday: Sorry I missed the game, I came down with the stomach flu last night.
examples.professional: Three people on the support team called in sick with stomach flu, so we pushed the release to Friday.
examples.analytical: Stomach flu, usually caused by norovirus, is a gastrointestinal infection rather than influenza, and that distinction matters for treatment and hygiene.

nuance.analogy: Stomach flu is like a storm that hits the digestive system instead of the lungs; the name flu borrows a term for a different kind of illness.
nuance.etymology: Stomach from Greek stomachos, and flu short for influenza, from Italian influenza.
common_mistakes: Assuming stomach flu is the same as influenza and needs a flu shot.
Using stomach flu for food poisoning without knowing the cause.
Pronouncing the flu with a long oo sound that is too stretched.

senses.definition: (rare) Strategic.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: Rare form meaning strategic; relating to strategy or a long-term plan for achieving a goal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the 'TI' syllable and keep the final 'al' reduced to a schwa and 'l'. Most speakers say it with three quick syllables after the stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds more formal or old-fashioned than 'strategic', so it can seem stiff or wordy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this form; 'strategic' is the normal word in almost every context. You will see it occasionally in older writing or in very formal prose, and using it in everyday speech can sound unnatural or like an error. Choose 'strategic' unless you are deliberately imitating a formal or old style.

distinctions.note: Both mean the same thing, but 'strategic' is the standard and far more common form in American English.
Strategical, like strategic, refers to the overall plan; tactical refers to the immediate methods used to carry it out.

examples.everyday: My dad's garage sale was almost strategical, with every box labeled and priced.
examples.professional: Her team's strategical review focused on the next three quarters rather than the current sprint.
examples.analytical: The historian's account is strategical rather than merely tactical, concerned with the purpose of each engagement.

nuance.analogy: Like an old map title: correct, but people now prefer the simpler modern label.
nuance.etymology: From strategy plus -ical, from Greek strategia, 'generalship'.
common_mistakes: Using it as the everyday word instead of 'strategic'.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the 'TI' syllable.

senses.definition: To lash out; to strike or hit at someone or something, particularly something in arm's length of the striker and at or near the level of the striker's head.
senses.example: When the drunk man lunged, Dave struck out with his fist and missed.

senses.definition: To strongly criticize or make a verbal attack, particularly as a response to previous criticism or provocation.
senses.example: After the senator's speech, critics struck out at his record on immigration.

senses.definition: To draw a line through some text such as a printed or written sentence, with the purpose of deleting that text from the rest of the document.
senses.example: Please strike out the old phone number and write the new one above it.

senses.definition: To treat something as settled.
senses.example: Let's strike out the debate about the merger; the vote is done and final.

senses.definition: To fail; to be refused a request or to have a proposal not be accepted, in particular a request for a (hopefully romantic) date.
senses.example: Dave asked the new girl to the dance but he struck out.

senses.definition: To begin to make one's way.
senses.example: The travelers struck out towards the line of mountains.

senses.definition: Of a batter, to be retired after three strikes (missed swings, as opposed to any other way of becoming "out"); of a pitcher, to cause this to happen to the batter.
senses.example: Jones struck out on a nasty slider.

core.definition: To set out on your own to begin something new; also to fail, or in baseball to be called out on strikes.

pronunciation.tip: The particle out carries the main stress, and the ow vowel should be a clear diphthong. The t in out is a crisp stop, so do not let it slide into the next word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it means starting out independently; negative when it means failing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say strike out on your own to describe leaving a job or group to start something independently, and strike out is also common in baseball and everyday talk about failing. Americans might also say the word for crossing out text, but the main everyday sense is independence. A natural reply is Good for you, or a question about the new plan.

distinctions.note: Lash out means to attack angrily with words or blows, while strike out in the independence sense means to set out on your own.
Cross out is a plain everyday phrase for deleting text, while strike out is more formal or technical in that sense.
Give up means to stop trying, while strike out often implies a fresh start or a brave new direction.

collocations: strike out in a new direction
struck out in the ninth inning

examples.everyday: After ten years at the same firm, Dana decided to strike out on her own.
